articles.title_orig: In Shanghai’s ‘Science City,’ China’s ascendant biotechs make their pitch to the world
articles.title_zh: In Shanghai’s ‘Science City,’ China’s ascendant biotechs make their pitch to the world
articles.content_orig:
This story is republished from STAT , the health and medicine news site that’s a partner to the Globe. Sign up for STAT’s free Morning Rounds newsletter here .
SHANGHAI — The biotech executives appeared triumphant.
It was a balmy, overcast Sunday here in the glimmer-and-glass “Science City” district, and the four leaders were on stage at the ballroom level of the five-star Hilton, joking about how much faster, cheaper, and more efficient drug development was here in China than anywhere else — certainly than the United States. (And God help Europe.)
Zhui Chen, cofounder of the now $6 billion Shanghai-based biotech Abbisko, recalled running a trial on a drug licensed to the German pharma Merck KGaA. Abbisko’s trial finished in 11 months, so quickly that Merck executives asked if Abbisko could train their staff.
For two years, American labs and board rooms have been riven with excitement and anxiety over the vertiginous rise of Chinese biotech. Almost overnight, it seemed, a half-century of American dominance in life sciences had evaporated. Big Pharma executives in New Jersey and New York scrambled to license drugs from Chinese companies few American scientists had ever heard of, hoping to find the next blockbuster to fill their balance sheet. Founders and investors in South San Francisco and Kendall Square watched their companies get passed over — or fold altogether — and wondered if they had a future.
To plant its own flag, Jefferies, the New York investment bank, convened its first Shanghai-based conference. The rationale was simple. The largest US life science conference is J.P. Morgan’s San Francisco summit. The largest European conference is held by Jefferies in London. China is still up for grabs.
On the main stage, panelists debated artificial intelligence, obesity, geopolitical tensions, American innovation versus Chinese execution, and the best way to commercialize a drug. Many pleaded for collaboration, not competition.
Executives walked through their pipelines in English, flashing antibody drugs in full Revlon counter variety. Local representatives from hulking multinationals like GSK, Merck, and Sanofi roamed the halls, scouting potential prospects. A contingent from SK Biopharmaceuticals, the Korean pharma, filled an elevator.
Even longtime veterans of the drug industry here struggled to make sense of what they’re seeing.
“It’s really blowing like everyone’s mind, right?” said Betty Huang, who helps spearhead Chinese business development for the German pharma Bayer.
Behind closed doors, a new wave of deals were coming to the fore. Cui Cui, Jefferies’s head of health care research for Asia, told local media that investors had traveled from Brazil and South America. The Shanghai conference was appended to a broader Asia tour, and Cui said she had met with representatives from a Texas teachers’ pension fund in Korea who “are very interested in China” — though they can’t invest for “various reasons.”
Venrock and other US VC firms had staff on site, talking trades and scoping out local operations. One US-based investor was trying to decide if they needed to hire someone in the region full time. Michael Garrow, chief investment officer of HS Group, a Hong-Kong based investment firm that backs specialized hedge funds, was meeting with portfolio managers to see if it was time to reinvest. Could he find “the RTW or RA Capital of Asia?” he said, naming prominent US health care funds.
A decade ago, health care-focused firms had popped up and flamed out in Asia. But now, there seemed to be “real innovation,” he said.
It was a well-timed summit. Two days before kickoff, the Chinese government issued its latest five-year-plan for biotech. By 2030, it wrote, Chinese drug developers should have at least five blockbuster drugs. One fourth of all first-in-class drugs should come out of China.
Bold, to say the least. Today, Chinese drugmakers have one or two blockbusters.
It’s hard, though, to see the latest frenzy of dealmaking and see anything but a diagonal line pointing up. The numbers vary, depending on which bank, consulting firm, or analyst you trust. But Chinese-designed drugs now make up about a third of the world’s pipeline and draw more than half of all licensing or collaboration deals, as measured by total dollar value.
Morgan Stanley seems to be a believer, projecting Chinese-designed drugs will account for 35 percent of all Food and Drug Administration approvals by 2040, compared to 5 percent today. So is Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla, who warned an Atlantic Council audience recently that the gravity had already shifted.
“I don’t want to lose the superiority of the US biopharma to the Chinese, which I see that happening in five years,” he said. “I don’t want that to happen. But we are putting 80 percent of our energy to think how to slow them down rather than 80 percent of our energy to see how we can become better than them.”
The Chinese government has been trying to steward biotech here for years, with mixed success. In the 2000s, large pharmas like GSK and Novartis set up R&D centers here, but most of them ultimately pulled back, with little to show for the lucre spent.
Most observers point to 2015 as the pivotal moment. The government started speeding review of new trials and approvals and brought its clinical trial system in line with international standards. In 2018, the Hong Kong stock exchange allowed unprofitable companies to go public, thus boosting biotech fundraising and VC returns.
Meanwhile, Chinese contract research organizations and manufacturing companies, like Wuxi AppTec, grew remarkably efficient, in part by working with American companies. Local scientists learned drug development inside these CROs, or the local divisions of Big Pharma. Or they trained abroad and came home.
American companies still work with the CROs, which are tightly woven into the ecosystem here. “A Chinese scientist who is using a CRO can just ride a bike and supervise them on how to do the science,” said one prominent Chinese biotech venture capitalist. “Unlike sitting in Boston, where you send an email and they respond a day later.”
Meanwhile, companies can enroll patients faster because large hospitals attract thousands of patients for care.
The result is companies that can engineer molecules every which way with ruthless efficiency and put them into early development on the cheap. After mastering generics, companies moved on to me-too-drugs, then me-better, and now are competing with US companies to develop more novel compounds.
Today, the old GSK building is occupied by Abbisko, beside other local pharma companies in an office park that features a KFC and Starbucks. Their scientists, typically making around 50 percent of what a US scientist would make, contribute to a system that is about 50 percent to 70 percent faster than the rest of the world in developing trial-ready molecules and then two to five times faster at recruiting patients for late-stage trials, per McKinsey estimates .
Ying Huang, who steered the Chinese-founded startup Legend Biotech as it beat out US competitors to develop a powerful cancer cell therapy Carvykti, sat on the same panel as Chen, the Abbisko cofounder. He said his distressed Boston colleagues complain that office and lab space in Kendall Square is vacant and they can’t get funding.
“We all know that this is the competition,” said Huang, who lives in New Jersey and now runs a startup licensing molecules out of China. “Whoever is more innovative, whoever is more efficient, will get investment.”
For all the fanfare, few thought — or at least would say — that the US biotech industry would wither away. Kendall Square would survive, assured Eric Liu, managing director of Banyan BioInnovations, a new China-focused offshoot of the life sciences investment bank Locust Walk.

articles.title_orig: World-class mentalist to perform in Bucksport
articles.title_zh: World-class mentalist to perform in Bucksport
articles.content_orig:
Internationally acclaimed mentalist Steve Taubman will bring his show “Mind Magic: A Night of Laughter and Astonishment” to the Alamo Theatre in Bucksport on Thursday, Oct. 15, at 7 p.m.
The show promises to be an unforgettable evening of mentalism, mind reading and comedy.
Mind Magic is not a magic show in the traditional sense, according to a review in The Scene SD Magazine, a San Diego entertainment guide.
“This is unlike any show you’ve seen,” Taubman said in the review.
“It’s not defined by a single label but rather draws on a lifetime of work that’s designed to create not just laughter and astonishment, but some deep thought about how our minds work and how we can make better connections with ourselves, others, and the world around us.”
Taubman is a mentalist, stage hypnotist, author and mindfulness coach from Vermont.
Tickets are available at Eventbrite.com for $35 before fees. A special VIP experience costs $55 plus fees and includes a post-show private debrief.

articles.title_orig: Houthis claim strike on Aramco site as Yemen fighting intensifies
articles.title_zh: Houthis claim strike on Aramco site as Yemen fighting intensifies
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s Houthis have said they attacked an Aramco facility in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government intensifies.
In a statement posted on X on Saturday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had carried out a “military operation with ballistic missiles and drones” that targeted Aramco in Riyadh.
He claimed the strikes were “precise and direct” and “led to fires breaking out” at the site. A large plume of smoke and fire was seen rising near an Aramco facility in Riyadh on Saturday.
Later on Saturday, Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, said in remarks carried by Saudi media that the Houthi claims of targeting Riyadh were “misleading”.
Early on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said its armed forces carried out 97 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.
Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemen’s government forces, said the attacks targeted “at least 260 Houthi fighters and destroyed or disabled 44 military vehicles”.
Late last month, the Houthis said they had attacked Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a Red Sea port on Saudi Arabia’s west coast.
Saudi Arabia said at the time it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired towards Taif and Yanbu and reported no damage to Aramco sites.
Earlier this week, the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis attacked a power station in the Muslim holy city of Medina on Tuesday.
The fighting has intensified since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July.
In mid-September, the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital route for global oil shipments, before anti-Houthi forces stabilised front lines.
Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced since fighting restarted.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the Yemeni government to retreat to Aden.

articles.title_orig: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel, will it curb prices?
articles.title_zh: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel, will it curb prices?
articles.content_orig:
The Group of Seven (G7) countries have agreed to release 100 billion barrels of crude oil and diesel from emergency reserves over several months in an effort to reduce soaring energy prices after pressure from United States President Donald Trump.
The US and Israel’s war on Iran, as well as Russia’s war on Ukraine, have triggered a spike in global oil and diesel prices.
“The emergency release by G7 members will put some downward pressure on prices, particularly global diesel prices. However, the impact would be short-lived given that this is just a temporary solution to the supply crunch,” Hamad Hussain, a climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told Al Jazeera.
Oil prices ‌jumped on Thursday and settled up more than $4 a barrel. Global diesel prices also hit a record high last Friday with the average price for a gallon (3.79 litres) of diesel at $6.50, up from $5.61 a month earlier, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
In a statement on Thursday, the G7, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the US, with the European Union also represented, said there will also be a “substantial diesel release within the first 20 days” and discussions over “additional diesel releases as necessary” will be held in the coming days.
Will the G7’s energy release stabilise the global energy market?
After a video conference of G7 leaders chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday, the group said in a joint statement: “Taking into account commitments that have already been fulfilled, we will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels.”
Earlier this week, the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Executive Director Fatih Birol said that members had released about two-thirds of the 400-million-barrel agreement.
The G7 energy release will begin immediately and last for four months and will include a substantial diesel release for 20 days. It is not clear how many oil and diesel stocks each member of the group will release.
“We will convene in the context of the IEA in the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary,” the statement said.
“We will coordinate maintenance schedules across G7 refineries to prevent simultaneous capacity shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where feasible,” it added.
The G7 also urged member countries to refrain from imposing export restrictions on energy products among themselves.
Earlier this week, the Trump administration had threatened to impose a ban on US diesel exports and also pressured Europe to release its emergency diesel stocks to help ease soaring diesel prices.
Global energy prices have been soaring due to the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which has disrupted energy exports from the Gulf. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy installations have also disrupted global energy supplies.
The former head of the International Energy Agency’s Oil Industry and Markets Division, Neil Atkinson, told Al Jazeera that there are three key factors contributing to the decline in global diesel supply.
First, “there isn’t diesel coming out of the Middle East to Europe, and Europe took quite a lot of diesel from Saudi Arabia and from Kuwait”.
Second, “Russia has now ceased to export diesel at all” due to “the attacks by Ukraine on Russian refineries”.
“And China is no longer exporting diesel,” he added.
“We’re in a situation where demand remains relatively high and is likely to stay high because of the agricultural harvesting season.”
According to data from the Joint Organizations Data Initiative (JODI) and the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), the US is the world’s largest producer and exporter of diesel. It produces about 240.5 million tonnes and exports around 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day.
Russia is the world’s second-largest diesel exporter, supplying 783,400 barrels per day (bpd) to the global market. Saudi Arabia is the world’s second-largest producer of diesel at 58.4 million tonnes, but it consumes a large portion of its diesel domestically.
After the G7 announcement, French President Macron, who had co-chaired the meeting, said the group’s move to release the oil will “bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.
The price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, briefly dropped below $100 a barrel after the G7 announcement, but rose to about $102 in the evening.
Naeem Aslam, chief investment officer at Zaye Capital Markets, told Al Jazeera that the G7 energy release was “very much needed”, but the group’s announcement was just to ease off pressure on the energy market.
“The actual structure changes about who is going to release [the energy stocks] and what and where the bans will be lifted, remains an important component in terms of the market,” he said.
Aslam added that by Sunday night, especially before the markets open, the added pressure on energy prices will come off. “But going into Monday morning … we could potentially see the reversal in the market,” he added.
Atkinson, the energy expert, said the G7’s fuel release is welcome but “doesn’t deal with the fundamental problem that the global supply remains lower than normal”.
Atkinson told Al Jazeera that “seven months after this war started in the Middle East, we are still in a situation where the global supply of crude oil or products remains significantly below pre-war levels”.
“We are now in a situation where the focus is on end use of products, mainly diesel, which is what we’re talking about here,” he added.
Soaring diesel prices have been a source of tension for the Trump administration and Republicans who fear this will cost them votes in the upcoming November midterm elections.
Last week, Trump pressured Ukraine to stop attacking Russian diesel facilities amid the war.
Then, on Thursday this week, the US president told reporters that his administration “may” ask European countries to release diesel stocks, shortly after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Europe to “immediately” tap its reserves.
Trump also threatened to ban US diesel exports if Europe did not release emergency diesel stocks.
But on Friday, Trump told reporters at the White House that Washington would not impose a diesel export ban. He said the plan was never really on the table.
“Europe has a lot of diesel, and they’re going to be making a major world contribution, and so are we. And we’re not going to be doing the export ban. We’re going to be doing what we’re supposed to do,” Trump said.
“Trump is scared by diesel prices above $6, which is a price jump of 70 percent compared to before he started the war. This is likely to get worse with US diesel inventories at their lowest seasonal level since records began in 1982.
“So if there is not enough diesel being produced because of the US-Israeli war on Iran, and diesel reserves have been used up, the only way to bring more diesel to the US market is by exporting less,” Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, told Al Jazeera on Friday.
After the G7 announcement, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform: “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately.”
The White House is also reportedly preparing an executive order to tackle record-high US diesel prices that could be unveiled as early as next week, two people familiar with the process told the Reuters news agency.
Schneider noted that countries are also concerned about high energy prices since diesel and gasoline are important for economies and fulfil different roles.

articles.title_orig: Tens of thousands protest against Spain's housing crisis following eviction of 87-year-old woman
articles.title_zh: Tens of thousands protest against Spain's housing crisis following eviction of 87-year-old woman
articles.content_orig:
Demonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to pass
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities as they step up demands for action to tackle ⁠a mounting housing crisis ⁠after ​government measures were struck down by the opposition.
Demonstrators on Saturday waved posters calling for a general strike ⁠after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in ⁠Madrid, and other housing issues, were rejected in parliament on ​Friday.
Authorities said 70,000 people were protesting. Organisers put the figure at 500,000.
“It’s a shame,” Nando ‌de Anguulo, 26, ‌who joined the protest in Madrid, told Reuters. “It only proves that it ‌is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, may call a snap election for November after the ‌legislation failed to pass, Spanish media reported on Friday, and would be watching the strength of Saturday’s ​protests before making a decision.
The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta .
Protests on Saturday were peaceful in 50 Spanish cities. In the south-eastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and teargas ⁠to break up the protests.
About 30 people managed to get inside ​the City ​of Arts and Sciences, a ​landmark cultural building in the city, before they were ​ousted by ‌police.
One protester in Madrid, Marcos Sainz, a librarian, 26, said he used to rent a two-bedroom apartment with friends for a monthly rent of 900 euros ($1,000) but that a one-bedroom flat often now cost 1,000 euros – or half the median monthly salary in the capital.
He told AFP he would protest rental spikes “until someone dares to regulate it all, as (otherwise) we’ll all have to leave Madrid and that would be a shame as I am from Madrid”.
Javier, 31, a solar panel installer, said: “We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project.” He added: “I spend half of my salary on a tiny room.”
“What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, an energy that is showing that eight days of people power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government,” Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants’ Union organising the protest, said in a statement.
“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” she said.
after newsletter promotion
Late on Saturday groups of far-right protesters, some of them performing Nazi salutes, tried to get to the camp in Madrid but were blocked by police.
One video posted on the website of Spanish daily El País showed police chasing some members of the group through the streets and the newspaper also reported that officers had made three arrests.
On Friday, Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
Despite the anger of the protesters outside parliament, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees.
The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building ​more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.
News of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.
The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years . The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: China Isn’t Building a New World Order. It’s Building a Majority in the Old One
articles.title_zh: China Isn’t Building a New World Order. It’s Building a Majority in the Old One
articles.content_orig:
BRICS can't agree on a currency and the SCO can't agree where to put its bank. Beijing doesn't need them to. What it wants from the Global South is votes, markets and a story, and it will cash them in at the UN, the IMF and the WTO.
Stalling Clubs, Growing Caucus
In mid-September Xi Jinping made his first visit to India in seven years for the BRICS summit in New Delhi. The bloc’s declaration opposed “unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures” without naming the United States. It softened last year’s language on the Middle East and once again stopped short of a common currency. Two weeks earlier in Bishkek, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation amended its charter but left its long-promised development bank stuck in a quarrel between Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan over which of them would host it. In the same weeks, Beijing said that about 160 countries and organisations now back its Global Governance Initiative, and that more than 60 have joined a “Group of Friends” meeting in New York, Geneva and Vienna, the UN’s three main seats. The clubs China helped build are stalling, while the caucus it is building inside the UN keeps growing. That contrast is the clearest answer yet to what Beijing wants.
Four Initiatives and a Retreating America
Xi launched the Global Governance Initiative on 1 September 2025 at the SCO summit in Tianjin, timed to the UN’s 80th anniversary. Its five principles — sovereign equality, international rule of law, “true” multilateralism, a people-centred approach and a focus on results — complete a set with Beijing’s earlier development, security and civilisation initiatives. Steve Tsang of SOAS calls this the Global South half of Xi’s “double pivot” . BRICS, meanwhile, has grown to 11 members and ten partner countries.
Stay ahead of the geopolitical week.
MD Briefing delivers expert analysis across five global fronts — the Indo-Pacific, energy, geoeconomics, European security, and the Middle East — every Monday morning. Free.
Two shifts changed the backdrop. The first is American retreat: in January Washington announced it would leave 66 international organisations . The second is China repositioning itself inside existing bodies. In September 2025 Premier Li Qiang said China would no longer seek special and differential treatment , the softer WTO rules reserved for developing countries, in future agreements, while keeping its developing-country status. And since 1 May 2026, goods from 53 African countries have entered China tariff-free .
Recruit Outside, Win Inside
The debate is usually framed as a choice: is China building a rival order, or reforming the existing one from within? The evidence of the past year points clearly to the second. Beijing is not trying to replace the UN, the IMF or the WTO. It is trying to win a durable majority inside them, and it uses BRICS and the SCO to recruit that majority, not to house it.
Look at where the effort goes. The Group of Friends meets in UN cities, not in Shanghai. China’s nine stated reform priorities lead with strengthening the UN and the authority of the Security Council, and Beijing has made more African representation on the Council an explicit goal. The one new international body it has created, the International Organization for Mediation in Hong Kong, is a mediation service that sits alongside existing courts and tribunals rather than competing with them. At this year’s WTO ministerial in Yaoundé, which collapsed over the rules for developing countries, it was Washington that attacked the system’s foundations and Beijing that defended “true multilateralism” .
The reason is simple: the existing institutions hold the prize. At the IMF, China’s actual quota share is 6.39% , less than half the 13.7% that the Fund’s own formula says its economy justifies. The US share of 17.4% preserves Washington’s veto over decisions that need 85% support. A parallel fund cannot break that veto or confer that legitimacy. Only votes inside the IMF can. Trade tells the same story. China ran a record $1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025 on exports of $3.77 trillion. A country that sells that much abroad needs open markets under predictable rules, not a world broken into rival blocs.
The weakness of BRICS and the SCO is therefore not a failure of Chinese strategy. It is evidence of what the strategy is. If Beijing wanted an alternative order, a bloc that cannot agree on a currency and a security organisation that cannot site a bank would be the flimsiest possible foundations, especially with India inside both, ready to slow anything that looks like a Chinese project. As recruiting grounds and test beds — for local-currency lending through the New Development Bank, or for links between national payment systems — they work well enough.
So what does Beijing want from the Global South? Votes, markets and a story. It wants votes to reweight the IMF, to defend developing-country rules at the WTO and to win Security Council seats for African states that would rarely vote against China. It wants markets to absorb the exports America no longer takes. And it wants a story in which China, not the US, is the defender of the UN Charter. The Africa zero-tariff scheme shows how cheaply some of this can be bought: the continent already runs a large trade deficit with China, so the gesture costs Beijing little and earns it a great deal. Giving up new WTO concessions while keeping developing-country status is the mirror image. It removes an American talking point without leaving the Global South club.
The strongest objection is that “reform from within” is cover. China has also built its own cross-border payments network, a digital currency, lenders such as the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, and now a mediation body it hosts. On this view, these are the skeleton of an exit. Part of that is right: Beijing is building plumbing that would survive Western sanctions. But plumbing built to survive sanctions is insurance, not a destination. The bigger threat to China’s strategy is its own export machine. In January Mexico imposed tariffs of up to 50% on 1,463 product lines from countries without a trade deal with it, China first among them. The surplus that pays for the courtship is also what is alienating the countries being courted.
Three Paths for Beijing’s Majority
Base case: incremental capture (about 55%). The Group of Friends keeps growing, Chinese candidates win more posts in UN agencies, and Beijing leads the push to rewrite the IMF quota formula. BRICS and the SCO stay modest. The key assumption is that the US stays disengaged and that Global South trade friction with China remains limited to sectors such as steel and cars. For Western governments and companies, Chinese influence will show up first in standard-setting fights inside UN technical agencies on AI, data and telecoms, long before it shows up in any new bloc.
Downside for Beijing: a Global South trade backlash (about 25%). Chinese goods diverted from the US flood a second wave of markets, and Brazil, Indonesia, South Africa or India follow Mexico with broad tariff increases rather than case-by-case anti-dumping duties. Votes become transactional, and BRICS splits along trade lines, with India leading a camp that treats China as a competitor first. The clearest early signal would be a large developing economy filing a WTO case against Chinese industrial subsidies.
Alternative: reform by inheritance (about 20%). If Washington’s retreat deepens, through further cuts to the UN’s regular budget or a walk-away from what remains of WTO dispute settlement, China becomes the main sponsor of a weakened existing system rather than its reformer. That would hand Beijing the order without having to rebuild it, but also its bills: development finance, peacekeeping and crisis lending that China has so far preferred to provide on its own terms.
Watch Bangkok, Not Bishkek

articles.title_orig: Elena Rybakina and Aryna Sabalenka, WTA world No. 1 and No. 2, out of China Open
articles.title_zh: Elena Rybakina and Aryna Sabalenka, WTA world No. 1 and No. 2, out of China Open
articles.content_orig:
Aryna Sabalenka was swatted aside in straight sets by 34th-ranked Nikola Bartunkova in the third round of the China Open, leaving the event without its top two seeds as world number one Elena Rybakina was ousted in the second round.
Czech player Bartunkova, 20, sent down four aces to beat the former world number one 6-4, 6-3 in one hour and 35 minutes on Sunday.
“I focused on myself, to be calm,” Bartunkova said.
“She’s a legend … so I’m really happy that I won the match,” she said of the four-time Grand Slam champion.
Bartunkova next faces Austria’s Sinja Kraus in the round of 16.
Second-seeded Sabalenka squandered five chances to break serve in the sixth game of the first set, with Bartunkova strong on defence and firing deep.
The 28-year-old from Belarus threw on a cap for the eighth game of the first set as the women switched between playing in the shade and the sun, but it did not turn the tide in her favour.
A frustrated Sabalenka tossed her racquet at a break down in the fourth game of the second set, and lost on the first match point when she returned into the net.
Earlier on Saturday, Elena Rybakina – who replaced Sabalenka as the world number one last month – was ousted by Alina Charaeva in the second round.
Top seed Alexander Zverev was scheduled to play Novak Djokovic later on Sunday in the quarterfinals of the men’s 500-level event also taking place.
The 39-year-old Serbian great enters the match with an extraordinary unbeaten streak in Beijing, but Zverev — last month’s US Open champion — is in the running for the top men’s ranking.

articles.title_orig: China's railway passenger trips hit record single-day high
articles.title_zh: China's railway passenger trips hit record single-day high
articles.content_orig:
Passengers line up at the boarding gates at Shenzhen North Railway Station in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, October 1, 2026. /VCG
China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on October 1, the first day of the week-long National Day holiday, setting a new single-day record, China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said Friday.
On October 2, the railway network is expected to handle 20.39 million passenger trips, with 1,462 additional trains scheduled to meet the high demand, the company said.
Passenger ticket pre-sales show that the most popular departure cities on Friday include Beijing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Nanjing, while popular arrival cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Shanghai, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou, Nanjing and Changsha.
Routes such as Xi'an-Chengdu round trips, as well as those from Beijing to Shenyang, Zhengzhou and Qingdao are among the busiest.
Railway authorities across the country have strengthened transport organization and implemented measures to ensure safe, convenient and comfortable travel.
China Railway Taiyuan Group has coordinated with local transport departments and scenic spots to add shuttle buses linking Datong South Station with the Yungang Grottoes, a UNESCO World Heritage site featuring more than 50,000 Buddhist stone sculptures, and the Hengshan Mountain scenic area in north China's Shanxi Province.
China Railway Hohhot Group has added 11 multiple-unit trains to the Baotou-Wuhai section of the Baotou-Yinchuan high-speed railway.
China Railway Wuhan Group, tapping the newly opened Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway, has launched a promotion campaign with local governments in Yichang and Xingshan, offering passengers exclusive discounts at scenic spots, hotels and homestays when they present their train tickets.
China Railway expects some 284 million passenger trips during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, which runs from September 23 to October 8.

articles.title_orig: 4-H Stream Team brings the fair to the world
articles.title_zh: 4-H Stream Team brings the fair to the world
articles.content_orig:
Stream Team members prepare to document a livestock showing at the Kootenai County Fair. Photo courtesy University of Idaho
Savanna Meyer, of Rathdrum, logged more than 20 volunteer hours on behalf of the 4-H Stream Team, livestreaming events during fair week at the 2026 Kootenai County Fair. Photo courtesy University of Idaho
Members of Teresa Balderrama’s 4-H Stream Team work behind the scenes and don’t receive awards or ribbons at county fairs.
Instead, their work spotlights the accomplishments of fellow 4-H members while connecting families and communities to fair competitions and other 4-H events through livestreams, videos and digital storytelling.
Balderrama is an educator at the University of Idaho Extension in Kootenai County. Her Stream Team, also known as the Digital Media Club, is an informal media team of youth from across the state who meet virtually at 7 p.m. PT on Mondays to coordinate coverage of University of Idaho Extension 4-H Youth Development events.
Thousands of 4-H’ers, along with their friends and family members, regularly view content on the Stream Team’s YouTube page, 4-H STEM on the Street. Team members gain valuable workforce skills in interviewing, storyboarding, photography, videography, technology operation and digital content production.
The Stream Team’s livestreams of 4-H livestock showings at northern Idaho county fairs provide an especially valuable service. Officials at one fair considered hiring a professional streaming service but stuck with the Stream Team when the bid came back at more than $10,000.
This fair season, the team streamed more than 88 hours of livestock shows at the Bonner, Boundary, Latah and Kootenai county fairs, and a team member made a video highlighting general events at the Benewah County Fair. The livestreams drew 6,044 viewers, not including those who watched recordings after the fact.
“It kind of hits a niche of kids who are not livestock kids, and they are not sewing kids,” Balderrama said. “They just love digital media.”
About 20 4-H members regularly participate in Stream Team. The team is especially popular among homeschooled 4-H members.
“It’s definitely a confidence boost, making you more confident with technology,” said Stream Team member Savanna Meyer, a sophomore at Lakeland Senior High School in Rathdrum. “We get to walk around with these microphone headsets and we feel really cool.”
The Stream Team began during the COVID-19 pandemic, when a group of youth used cell phones and tablets to livestream northern Idaho 4-H fair competitions for friends and family who couldn't attend because of social distancing restrictions.
The streams were well received, and in 2022, Balderrama secured $540,800 in federal American Rescue Plan Act stimulus funding, awarded through the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare, to purchase video equipment. She built a wooden table on wheels, which her team uses to roll video equipment to livestock arenas for filming shows.
Her videographers use a joystick to control multiple cameras at once.
“A lot of the Stream Team members do show animals, too, but it also gives the kids who normally wouldn’t have a reason to be at the fair an opportunity to be a part of it,” Balderrama said.
During the 2026 Kootenai County Fair, Meyer showed a 4-H goat and a dairy heifer she raised as an FFA project while also exhibiting a 4-H veterinary science poster. Helping the Stream Team set up equipment and operate cameras gave her something productive to do when she wasn’t in the show ring. During fair week, Meyer logged about 20 volunteer hours with the team.
“If I have time to be on my phone, then I have time for another thing,” said Meyer, who plans to become a large animal veterinarian. “It also looks good on a college or job application to say, ‘I know how to run a soundboard, and I know how to run software programs.’
Thanks to the livestreams, many parents who cannot leave work can still watch their children compete. Many 4-H’ers who show animals review recordings to evaluate their performances and identify opportunities for improvement.
The broadcasts are especially popular with out-of-town relatives. At the Latah County Fair, Balderrama heard about grandparents who couldn’t attend their grandchild’s 4-H show in person because of a flight cancellation, but watched the livestream from Texas. She also learned of a grandmother in Dublin, Ireland, who tuned in to watch her grandchildren show dairy cows.
The Stream Team livestreams 14 livestock shows at each fair, as well as the market sale. Youth in northern Idaho with access to the video equipment have also livestreamed a high school football game, an Ironman triathlon, junior rodeos and a speaker at the annual Idaho 4-H Know Your Government Conference. Team members also produce a regular 4-H STEM on the Street podcast, as well as videos, video shorts and news reels covering major 4-H events.
Stream Team members from other regions of the state who can’t access the team’s equipment use their own cell phones and tablets to capture footage and access free editing and graphics-production software and apps.
One Bonneville County member plans to produce a video with an insider’s perspective of the annual Idaho 4-H Learn, Engage, Act, Develop (I-LEADS) Summit. Balderrama often recruits new Stream Team members during the Idaho 4-H State Teen Association Convention in Moscow, where she presents a workshop on making news reels and creating social media content. She also promotes the program to students at the Know Your Government Conference, where she works with 4-H members assigned to play the roles of legislative reporters.
During fair week, Meyer and her peers seek out 4-H members who seem bored to pitch in and help with streaming, which has been one of the most effective ways to grow the program.
“A lot of kids just sit around the fair or just go home, but if you have Stream Team, you have something to look forward to,” Meyer said. It really helps kids get out of their comfort zones. It’s not fully throwing them to the wolves with public speaking, but it’s helping them work as a team, because we couldn’t do it with any one person.”
John O’Connell, University of Idaho College of Agricultural and Life Sciences.

articles.title_orig: ‘Adua’ Collaboration Is Born From a Flower Between Worlds
articles.title_zh: ‘Adua’ Collaboration Is Born From a Flower Between Worlds
articles.content_orig:
Artwork by Karen Paulina Biswell & Maria Amilbia Siagama Siagama
Words by Karen Paulina Biswell
My collaboration with María Amilbia Siagama Siagama began 15 years ago, when I met her daughter in the streets of Bogotá, and continued into the mountains of Risaralda. It has been driven by curiosity, the desire to know one another, and learning to accept the opacity and misunderstandings that run through our relationship.
Our joint project, ADUA , takes its title from the Embera word for “I don’t know”—an embrace of uncertainty that offers a form of kinship that doesn’t erase difference, but learns to live with and through it. It also makes space for what does not need to be translated or explained.
My conversations with María Amilbia led me to the Benakúa ceremony, where men of knowledge drink a preparation made from the Brugmansia flower and travel to the underworld. For the Emberá, getting drunk and dreaming are intertwined: seeing and dreaming can become the same experience. What interested me was this idea of “knowing through forgetting.” What would it mean to forget the ways we had learned to see Indigenous communities? For me, it meant forgetting myself, opening myself to others, and allowing dreaming to become a way of seeing.
At the heart of ADUA is the Brugmansia, or iguaka, a sacred plant understood by the Emberá Chamí as a spiritual master and companion species. Its downward-facing flowers are associated with the world beneath us, a realm of knowledge and wisdom. In the Benakúa ceremony, the journey to this underworld can bring back guidance for tending the territory.
In these images, the Brugmansia becomes a kind of satellite between worlds—between seeing and dreaming, knowing and forgetting, memory and belief. It is through the flower that ADUA asks how we might encounter one another without needing to make everything fully known.

articles.title_orig: David Jackson wins third World 3D title as France triumph in Yankton
articles.title_zh: David Jackson wins third World 3D title as France triumph in Yankton
articles.content_orig:
France‘s David Jackson took a third World 3D title in barebow men after defeating Spain‘s Cesar Vera Bringas in the final at Yankton 2026 World Archery 3D Championships .
The 34-year-old previously won at the championships in 2019 and 2022, the same year he became world field champion.
The barebow women‘s title also went to France, with Virginie Chevrier triumphing at her maiden world championships, defeating reigning European champion Rosemarie Leitner of Austria.
The compound competition was won by Slovenia‘s Tim Jevsnik , defeating multiply decorated field and 3D champion Nico Wiener of Austria. The reigning European champion, France‘s Aude Ama-Cormerais defeated Ingrid Ronacher , another Austrian former champion, for the women‘s title.
Jackson was also part of France‘s four man men‘s team who also took gold at the event yesterday. The wins pushed France to the top of the medal table for the event, ahead of Austria and Russia.
The traditional bow titles went to Denmark‘s Zibrandt Christensen and Germany‘s Judith Wenzl. The latter is the reigning European champion and Christensen takes his second title after a win in 2017.
The individual longbow competition was won by Russia‘s Mikhail Poddevalin and Austria‘s Johanna Pitschmann , the latter one of the older competitors in the field, winning a world title age 63.
Pitschmann’s victory was perhaps less of a surprise to an unsighted bow field notable for the higher average age of the competitors – in a discipline where experience and learned instinct counts for a great deal.

articles.title_orig: Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
articles.title_zh: Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has continued rallying for Republican candidates while visiting Ohio, proposing a defiant outlook on his party’s chances in the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump told a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, that he believes there will be a “big surprise” in the upcoming elections, claiming his Democratic opponents do not know what is happening.
Polls have suggested that Democrats could gain ground in the midterms, but the US president said Republicans would do better than critics expect.
“Just get out and vote,” Trump said as he rallied for US Senator Jon Husted, gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and other Republicans.
“If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big,” he said.
Multiple incumbent Republican senators across the country face tough political headwinds, with Trump’s popularity falling in recent months as higher petrol prices and those for other staples persist amid the US-Israel war ⁠⁠on Iran.
Husted, a Republican in a competitive Ohio race against Democrat Sherrod Brown, hopes the president can motivate supporters who might otherwise skip midterm elections.
Trump garnered more than 55 percent of the Ohio vote in the 2024 presidential election, but economic concerns since then have sunk his approval ratings.
Ohio petrol prices increased 35 percent over the past year to $4.16 per gallon (3.8 litres) on average, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which compiles data ⁠⁠on automobile travel. Trump’s trade policy with Canada has also led to retaliatory Canadian tariffs that affect about $3bn worth of Ohio exports, based ⁠⁠on 2025 figures, Canadian broadcaster CBC reported.
Talking to reporters shortly before addressing Saturday’s rally, Husted said the US has to win the Iran war “on our terms” and, in the interim, he is “showing people that I’m fighting for lower prices”.
Trump extensively promoted his administration’s action on data centres, mainly those built for AI, during the rally, saying he was seeking to ensure they “benefit local communities” and praising Husted for an unsuccessful attempt to push forward legislation on the issue.
“Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” he said, repeating his defence of data centres.
Data centres have become a hot political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies.
The issue became especially acute in Ohio, where Husted has been repeatedly attacked for his role in attracting data centres to the Midwestern state as lieutenant governor.
The Republican-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this past week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats.
“Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centres in Ohio,” Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump’s visit. “Now, he’s making Ohioans foot the bill.”

articles.title_orig: Report says heat, fires left a third of the world living with 'extremely poor' air quality
articles.title_zh: Report says heat, fires left a third of the world living with 'extremely poor' air quality
articles.content_orig:
A European Union analysis released on Sept. 30 suggests that adding heat waves and wildfire smoke to existing air pollution has exposed about a third of the world's population to what it classified as "extremely poor" air quality.
Malay Mail reported that the European Union's Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service said 34% of people worldwide faced what it labeled "extremely poor" air quality from Jan. 1 through Sept. 15.
Another 17% of the global population fell into the "very poor" category, and only 5% reached what it described as "good" ozone levels.
Asia was hit the hardest, with 53% of the region's population in the "extremely poor" category and another 22% in "very poor" ozone conditions.
Those exposure categories were measured against World Health Organization guidance that caps eight-hour ozone exposure at 100 micrograms per cubic meter.
On hot, sunny days, pollution from vehicles, industry, and wildfires can react in the air to create ground-level ozone, a pollutant that can turn already polluted conditions into a major health risk.
Health effects can include damaged lung tissue, trouble breathing, and asthma attacks.
According to the analysis, record heatwaves and wildfires in Europe and North America helped drive the increase, with smoke spreading far beyond the burned areas.
Ozone has been especially hard to bring down, even as some other harmful pollutants have declined, because climate conditions make it easier to form. The analysis also pointed to major wildfires in Indonesia and said El Niño, which began in June, could contribute to more fires in Southeast Asia.
The Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service tracks pollution and wildfire activity using satellite data and computer models.
That helps explain why ozone remains a stubborn problem even after declines in some other major air pollutants over recent decades.
Dangerous air is not always local or visible. A stretch of hot, sunny weather combined with smoke or urban pollution can worsen air quality even far from a wildfire, making air-quality alerts more important during heat events.
As CAMS director Laurence Rouil said in the Atmosphere Watch report: "Air pollution does not stop at borders. It can travel thousands of kilometres, crossing continents and oceans and affecting air quality far from its source."
These stories look at the same ozone and smoke threats highlighted in this report.
• Across the U.S., blazing heat and wildfires are wiping out air quality gains .
• Across the U.S., wildfire-driven ozone is linked to premature deaths far from the flames.
• In China, scientists found that winter ozone pollution can spike even without summer heat.

articles.title_orig: I place the world's top software engineers and interviewed over 10,000 job seekers. The difference on paper and in person is wider than ever
articles.title_zh: I place the world's top software engineers and interviewed over 10,000 job seekers. The difference on paper and in person is wider than ever
articles.content_orig:
Paddy Lambros is founder and CEO of AI recruiter Dex.
Go to LinkedIn on any given day and you can read horror stories of hiring managers receiving thousands of AI-generated CVs, or applicants applying unsuccessfully for thousands of roles.
But while hiring is an undoubtedly dysfunctional process (one we are trying to fix, by the way) the main reasons that people don’t get hired existed long before AI.
Before I built an AI recruitment startup for software engineers, I worked in actual recruitment, finding the best tech talent for companies like Microsoft , Accenture , Deloitte.
I’ve interviewed thousands of applicants, and it is fair to say I’ve seen a few interview train-wrecks. But my main takeaway is that the reasons people don’t get hired are relatively simple – and avoidable – and that, as an applicant, you really have to do very little to stand out.
You can’t win on the strength of your CV, but you can lose.
If you send out a document that looks terrible, is full of spelling mistakes or doesn’t make sense, then you are sending a pretty negative signal of what you think good work looks like.
The main reason CVs fail is because they talk guff: “I conceptualised the Q3 planning process” or some such nonsense.
You need to be concrete: ‘I helped build X. I helped the company sell more Y’ or ‘This is what I did, and this is how it happened.’
You would not believe how many people fail at this point.
I’ve put out job specs for entry level roles and – at the bottom – given my email and asked candidates to reach out and tell me why they want the job. 90% of people don’t.
I remember putting out an advert for a very junior role with a box that said: ‘Tell me why you’d be great fit for this job’ and most people didn’t fill it in. It is baffling.
I always respond to people who write something interesting in that box. You need to act like you really want the job.
And if you are asked to do an exercise as part of the application process, then do it.
I’ve heard people say that they won’t work for free or are worried that the company will not hire them and steal their work, but honestly, it is a delusion.
If the company is interviewing people, then they really want to hire someone and they’re trying to work out if you could be that person.
If you really think you can produce better work in a couple of hours than the team working on it full time, then you’re either the best in the world or they are rubbish, in either case you probably shouldn’t be interviewing there.
You often see people claiming that they have applied for 1,000 jobs and got no responses: Well, nobody is qualified for 1,000 jobs. You are wasting your time.
Take that time and spend it researching five jobs and really putting the effort in.
I get that people are playing the volume game but most jobs that people are applying for they are either not qualified for – or aren’t right for them. But if they’d actually gone through the job spec, they’d realise that.
Hiring is a high-stakes game: 50% of new highs fail or quit in 18 months and only one in five new hires is considered a success after 12 months.
Consider the impact that has on a business: not only all the work – and cost – involved with finding the right candidate and hiring them, but the impact that an unsuccessful hire has on the rest of the team. This is all the more acute in startups, which tend to have very small teams.
So, when you walk into that job interview feeling nervous, remember that the person interviewing you may be just as nervous. They may have been through this a few dozen times already. They may have one or two bad hires behind them.
And remember it is a two-way street. The interviewer wants to get to know you, but you need to get a handle on this company too. Do you want to spend 80% of your waking hours here?
Honestly, one of the main reasons people fail an interview is because they are unable to answer this question.
I get that they are worried it will make them look bad, but it will make you look much worse if you can’t answer it.
It is inconceivable that your interviewer would never have made a mistake, so be honest, open up, and don’t turn this into an opportunity to blow your own trumpet.
There is nothing more valuable in hiring than a personal recommendation or a referral.
It should be a reminder that growing and maintaining your professional network is a key part of your career. You need to be a person others would vouch for.
And people don’t vouch for people just because they like them, they vouch for people who do a good job. They want to know that when they say: ‘You should hire this person’ and they do, you turn out really well.

articles.title_orig: Avelumab Effective Against Merkel Cell Carcinoma in Real-World Population, Despite Frequent AEs
articles.title_zh: Avelumab Effective Against Merkel Cell Carcinoma in Real-World Population, Despite Frequent AEs
articles.content_orig:
In a real-world cohort of older patients in Austria, avelumab (Bavencio) was determined to be effective for treating Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC), despite frequent adverse events (AEs).
“ Avelumab achieved clinically meaningful outcomes in this older, less-selected routine care cohort,” said first author Magdalena Forstinger, MD, a physician-researcher with Sigmund Freud Privatuniversität and Klinik Hietzing, Vienna. “Adverse events affected treatment in some patients, underscoring the importance of careful monitoring,” she added.
Forstinger presented the findings on October 2 at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) 2026 Congress in Vienna.
In 2017, avelumab, a programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1)-blocking antibody, became the first treatment approved by the FDA for MCC. The study abstract noted, however, that evidence of the drug’s efficacy and safety in a routine clinical care context was limited, particularly among older patients, a population more likely to be immunocompromised and have comorbidities, who are underrepresented in trials.
The nationwide, multicenter, retrospective chart review included patients with inoperable locally advanced or metastatic MCC who had received at least one cycle of avelumab, with no other exclusion criteria applied, Forstinger said. A total of 49 patients were included in the study, with a median age of 81 years (range, 62-96). The most common comorbidities were cardiovascular, metabolic, oncologic, and pulmonary.
The primary endpoint was real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS). Secondary endpoints included real-world overall survival (rwOS), objective response rate (rwORR), duration of response (rwDOR), and time to response (rwTTR), and safety.
At the start of treatment, 42.9% of participants had stage IIIB MCC and 57.1% had stage IV MCC. A total of 16.3% were immunocompromised or immunosuppressed, and 77.6% had an ECOG performance status ≤ 1. Avelumab was administered as first-line monotherapy in 77.6% of cases, with 22.4% also receiving other modalities such as radiotherapy. Median follow-up was 8.9 months (range, 0-73.1).
Nearly half of evaluable patients (n=48) responded to avelumab, Forstinger said, and median rwPFS, the primary endpoint, was 10.1 months (95% CI, 1.8-18.4). The rwORR was 47.9% (95% CI, 34.5-61.7), and median rwOS was 22.9 months (95% CI, 5.0-40.8). Median rwTTR was 3.9 months (range, 1.4-12.7), and median rwDOR among responders was 19.2 months (95% CI, 8.9-29.5).
Forstinger observed that rwPFS and rwOS were in a similar range to those reported in the 2021 phase 2 JAVELIN Merkel 200 trial (which evaluated first-line avelumab in patients with metastatic MCC), although rwORR was lower. JAVELIN did not include immunocompromised patients, she added.
Overall, 71.4% of patients experienced an AE and 53.1% experienced an immune- and/or treatment-related AE, including 24.5% who had a grade ≥ 3 AE. AEs led to treatment interruption or discontinuation in 28.6% of participants, including permanent discontinuation in 12.2% of cases.
Previously reported AEs for avelumab in patients with MCC include fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, infusion-related reactions, rash, nausea, constipation , cough, and diarrhea . Potentially serious immune-mediated adverse reactions include pneumonitis, colitis , hepatitis , endocrinopathies, nephritis with renal dysfunction, and dermatologic reactions.
In a post-hoc analysis, scores of ≤ 1 on the ECOG performance status scale, which describes a patient’s level of function, were associated with lower hazard ratios (HRs) for rwPFS (HR, 0.257; 95% CI, 0.100-0.658; P = .005) and rwOS (HR, 0.157; 95% CI, 0.047-0.521; P = .002). Forstinger said these findings should be interpreted as “hypothesis-generating.”
Forstinger has reported no relevant financial relationships.
Scott Harris has covered dermatology for more than a decade. He lives near Washington, DC.

articles.title_orig: Kathleen Turner shares baffled reaction to Michael Douglas’s affair confession
articles.title_zh: Kathleen Turner shares baffled reaction to Michael Douglas’s affair confession
articles.content_orig:

Kathleen Turner has responded after Michael Douglas confessed that they had an affair more than 40 years ago — and it’s pretty hilarious.
Douglas, 82, reveals in his new memoir One Helluva Ride that he and Turner began a secret relationship while filming the 1984 adventure movie Romancing the Stone in Mexico, despite both of them previously denying it. At the time, Douglas was separated from Diandra Luker, his first wife and the mother of his son Cameron.
After Douglas’s confession made headlines Friday, Turner told People in a statement: “Good heavens, what a fuss about something 40 years ago! I love Michael, and I look forward to enjoying the book.”
In an excerpt of the memoir published by the outlet, Douglas wrote that he “fell hard” for Turner while working together, and that he’d sneak into her room after the rest of the cast was asleep after long days on set.
Douglas said that they kept their affair hidden from everyone, including their co-star Danny DeVito and director Robert Zemeckis.
“Kathleen was smart, funny, and sexy with a deep, sultry voice that became her signature,” he wrote. “I instantly liked her, and we were immediately attracted to each other.”
He continued: “Things at home were in a bad place. Diandra and I were both having extramarital affairs... I left for Mexico still technically married, but separated.”
According to Douglas’s account, the romance ended when his wife visited the set and brought their son.
“Diandra grew suspicious,” he wrote. “A woman’s intuition, I suppose.”
He said that during the visit, Luker had reminded Turner that Douglas was still married. Turner did not want to interfere.
“After that visit, Kathleen and I ended things, and I went back to Diandra,” he said. “I did it for Cameron, but we shouldn’t have gotten back together. After that first split, it was never the same between us ever again.” The former couple went on to divorce in 2000.
Douglas married his current wife, Catherine Zeta-Jones, later that year. The pair have two children together : Dylan and Carys.
Turner and Douglas worked on several projects after Romancing the Stone, but continued to deny any relationship.
In an interview in 2023, Turner told The Guardian about Douglas: “I think we might have been falling in love. But then Diandra flew down and made it clear that she did not consider Michael to be available. So that ended that because I can’t get involved with another woman’s relationship. But oh my, that attention is delicious.”
When asked how close she came to dating Douglas, Turner replied at the time: “None of your business.”
Douglas wrote that he asked Turner for permission to include their romance in his book.

articles.title_orig: Searchers find debris of Boston-bound medical plane that went missing off Nantucket
articles.title_zh: Searchers find debris of Boston-bound medical plane that went missing off Nantucket
articles.content_orig:
Searchers found debris of a medical transport jet that vanished south of Nantucket early Saturday morning while flying from Bermuda to Boston, authorities said.
The six passengers and crew on board were still unaccounted for, a US Coast Guard spokesperson said Saturday night.
Coast Guard boats, planes, and helicopters launched the search off Nantucket after the transport flight disappeared early Saturday. Air traffic controllers in New York had struggled to communicate with the jet as it plunged toward the Atlantic Ocean.
“You’re coming in blind? Is that what you said?” a controller asked the pilot at about 12:46 a.m. “Are you declaring an emergency, or no?”
The pilot’s response, according to a recording captured by LiveATC.net, was not audible.
The airplane, a Gulfstream G100 that took off from Bermuda late Friday, was carrying a patient and family member as well as a four-person crew.
As the jet approached Nantucket, its pilot reported electrical failures, according to radio transmissions . Data from the website FlightAware show the plane descended thousands of feet within three minutes.
Shortly afterward, around 1 a.m., it disappeared from radar entirely.
The crew members are Canadian citizens and the passengers are Bermudian nationals, according to Clarence Togeretz, operations manager for Latitude Air Ambulance, the company in Ontario that operates the Gulfstream G100.
Steven MacKinnon, the leader of Canada’s public transportation agency, declined to identify the people on board the flight. The Bermuda Gazette reported that the two passengers aboard were a patient and their son.
In a statement, the Bermudian government said it was in touch with the families of the passengers and US search crews.
“We are praying that all six people will be found safe,” said Bermuda Premier David Burt.
The plane left L. F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda for the 800-mile flight to Boston at 11:41 p.m. on Friday, said Ciara Eve, an airport spokesperson. Bermuda, a self-governing British territory, is one hour ahead of Eastern Daylight Time.
As the jet descended toward the Atlantic, air traffic controllers asked to confirm whether they were declaring an emergency.
“You’re coming in a little weak so I didn’t hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not,” the air traffic controller said. He later confirmed the pilot declared an emergency, but struggled to reestablish contact with the aircraft.
The controller asked the pilot of a second plane whether the Gulfstream G100 aircraft was visible on its anti-collision system. But the second plane was flying at a much higher altitude and couldn’t pick up signs of jet, the pilot said.
For much of the flight, the Gulfstream jet traveled at about 24,000 feet, but at about 1:04 a.m., FlightAware data show the plane descended 13,000 feet within three minutes.
With the plane about 80 miles south of Nantucket at 1:06 a.m., a dispatcher at Logan International Airport directed crews to stage on the runway for the plane. She said it was due to land in 15 minutes and had lost “radio and radar,” according to radio transmissions captured by Broadcastify.
Emergency crews got into position and waited.
At 1:20 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration issued an alert, an agency spokesperson said. The plane wouldn’t land at Logan, and a search and rescue mission had been launched.
On the runway at Logan, the Massport Fire Rescue commander heard a radio transmission reporting that air traffic control said it could no longer see the plane on the radar.
“I don’t know if you monitored the tower radio, but the tower lost radar contact with this aircraft,” the commander radioed at about 1:36 a.m.
“Received, I do have it. I was listening,” the dispatcher said.
Emergency crews on the runway were ordered back to their headquarters. At 2 a.m., the FAA alerted the US Coast Guard of the missing plane.
On Nantucket, police checked the island’s airport for the missing jet but found nothing, said Lieutenant Angus MacVicar.
At sunrise, officers and the harbormaster began combing Nantucket’s southern shoreline aboard ATVs in search of signs of the plane, he said.
Governor Maura Healey said Saturday her “thoughts and prayers go out to all on board and all involved.”
“We’ll do whatever we can as a state to support efforts there and work with the Coast Guard,” Healey said at a labor rally in Dorchester.
Chris Van Buskirk and John R. Ellement of the Globe staff contributed to this report .
Laura Crimaldi can be reached at laura.crimaldi@globe.com . Follow her @lauracrimaldi . Rita Chandler can be reached at rita.chandler@globe.com . Camilo Fonseca can be reached at camilo.fonseca@globe.com . Follow him on X @fonseca_esq and on Instagram @camilo_fonseca.reports .

articles.title_orig: US Department of Justice indicts CEO for smuggling ‘AI chips’ into China
articles.title_zh: US Department of Justice indicts CEO for smuggling ‘AI chips’ into China
articles.content_orig:
A California technology entrepreneur accused of helping move more than $300 million worth of export-controlled computer servers to China is at the center of one of the largest recent U.S. cases involving advanced artificial intelligence hardware and export restrictions.
Federal authorities arrested Greg Lui, 38, on Thursday, alleging he orchestrated a scheme to send high-end computer servers containing advanced U.S.-made graphics processing units, or GPUs, to China through third countries in violation of federal export-control laws.
Lui, also known as Yiu Kong Lui, faces charges of conspiracy to violate export-control regulations, smuggling, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. If convicted on all counts, he could face up to 50 years in prison.
According to federal prosecutors, Lui owns Earthmade Computer Inc., a technology company based in the City of Industry in Los Angeles County.
Public business profiles show Earthmade was founded in 2021 and operated in areas including server procurement, technology infrastructure, and data-center services.
According to public profiles, Lui's technology career began with work in hosting and colocation services before he launched Earthmade Computer. The company marketed itself as a provider of server procurement, infrastructure, and data-center solutions, placing it in the fast-growing market for advanced computing hardware during the boom in artificial intelligence investment.
Before entering the technology sector, Lui was involved in the restaurant business. Public profiles indicate he helped launch a San Gabriel Valley restaurant specializing in Sichuan cuisine before later transitioning into technology and data-center operations.
Authorities allege Earthmade became the vehicle through which export-controlled AI hardware was purchased and routed overseas.
The Justice Department said Earthmade received more than $176 million from two Malaysia -based shipping companies between January and October 2024 as part of the alleged operation.
Newsweek has reached out to Earthmade via email for comment after regular business hours.
According to the indictment, Lui and his co-conspirators acquired export-controlled computer servers containing advanced GPUs commonly used in artificial intelligence applications.
Prosecutors say the operation relied on a practice known as transshipment, in which goods are routed through intermediate countries before reaching their final destination. U.S. authorities have increasingly focused on such arrangements as companies and individuals seek to evade export restrictions on advanced chips, servers and other technologies subject to national-security controls.
The government alleges the servers could not legally be exported directly to China without special licenses from the Commerce Department.
Instead, prosecutors say the equipment was shipped to countries including Malaysia and Singapore, where export restrictions were less stringent. Once there, the servers were allegedly forwarded to buyers in China.
Investigators also accuse Lui and others of providing U.S. manufacturers with false documentation that concealed the equipment's true destination.
One example cited in court filings involves a January 2024 purchase of 27 servers worth roughly $7.6 million, shipped from Los Angeles to Kuala Lumpur. Prosecutors say a co-conspirator later acknowledged that the servers had been forwarded to a China-based buyer.
The government alleges the broader operation moved more than $300 million worth of restricted technology.
The charges come as the United States continues tightening restrictions on advanced computer chips and AI-related hardware destined for China.
Washington has argued that the most sophisticated semiconductors and computing systems can be used for military, intelligence, and surveillance purposes, making them a national-security concern.
According to prosecutors, the servers involved in the case contained GPUs commonly used in advanced artificial intelligence systems, which the Trump administration now refers to as "Super Intelligence."
Assistant Attorney General John Eisenberg described AI chips as one of the country's most strategically important technologies.
Federal officials allege Lui knowingly circumvented export rules designed to prevent advanced American technology from reaching prohibited users.
The FBI, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, and the Defense Criminal Investigative Service are investigating.
Lui has been charged but not convicted. The allegations are contained in a federal indictment, and he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.
The federal court docket did not identify legal counsel for Lui, according to Bloomberg .
