articles.title_orig: Flydubai captain says copilot asked to pray, then struck him from behind; describes exactly how he opened cockpit door
articles.title_zh: Flydubai captain says copilot asked to pray, then struck him from behind; describes exactly how he opened cockpit door
articles.content_orig:
TEL AVIV — A Flydubai pilot attacked his flight captain using a crash ax and tried to take control of the aircraft’s controls in an attempted terrorist attack, an official with the United Arab Emirates said Saturday.
The suspect is Omani citizen Hamam al-Hammami, multiple sources from three agencies briefed on the investigation and a diplomat in the Middle East told NBC News. Authorities have not officially released the identity.
The Wall Street Journal, citing sources familiar with the matter, reported that al-Hammami had “previously been banned from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views.”
Oman Air did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether he previously worked for the company.
Emirati officials are leading investigations into the midair incident, which occurred Wednesday on a flight carrying 174 mostly Israeli passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv. A crash was averted, according to eyewitnesses and Israeli officials, when crew and passengers were able to enter the cabin and subdue the attacker.
“Investigations into the incident aboard Flydubai flight FZ1073 revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a terrorist act,” UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said in an update on Saturday.
“The co-pilot began executing his plan during the flight, attacking the captain inside the flight deck using a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls,” he said.
Al-Hammami was transferred from Saudi Arabia to Abu Dhabi on Thursday, the Saudi Interior Ministry said. The statement said his health had “improved,” but his medical condition was unclear.
Al Shamsi said investigations were ongoing to “establish the full circumstances, motives, and any links related to the incident.”
Israeli government spokesman David Mencer said Friday that Israeli investigators would “join their Emirati counterparts in investigating this attempted mass murder and establishing precisely what happened, his motives and background.”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday: “As time passes, the picture becomes clearer: The attacker had undergone Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane, along with its passengers.”
He did not say how he reached that conclusion, but added: “We are investigating whether he was sent, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price.”
Netanyahu’s spokesman Doron Spielman told NBC News that the suspect “talks on his social media about killing Jews.”
The flight captain, Indian national Capt. Smit Machchhar , spoke for the first time Friday from a hospital in Abu Dhabi.
Flydubai pilot speaks out follow mid-air attack
Machchhar was widely praised for his efforts to prevent the plane from crashing by opening the cockpit door and allowing passengers and crew members to rush in.
Speaking from his hospital bed, Machchhar said he had been “severely injured” and “could sense that the aircraft was going down.”
“I was acting for my own life, but at the same time, I knew I couldn’t let all of them die,” he said on a video call released by India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi, adding that he told himself to “give just one last push” to the cockpit door.
The Indian Embassy in Abu Dhabi called Machchhar the “Indian braveheart,” saying in an X post Saturday that he “remains under excellent medical care & is recovering well.”
The deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, Hamdan bin Mohammed, posted photos on X after visiting Machchhar in the hospital in which he’s seen kissing the pilot’s head and shaking his hand. Machchhar, with one arm in a cast and medical dressings on his head, appears awake and smiling.
“From us, and from the leadership of the nation, he has our full appreciation and praise,” he wrote.
Ayelet Epstein, a 47-year-old Israeli, told NBC News that her 14-year-old daughter asked if they were going to die when they heard shouting and “a huge fall started.”
“I told her, no, I don’t think so, we’re going to be OK,” she said, adding that “I was trying to rationalize things in a hopeful way for her.”
Epstein thanked Machchhar “from the bottom of my heart” for saving their lives, lauding his bravery.
A Flydubai spokesperson said Saturday: “We recognise that there are many questions at this stage; however, the circumstances surrounding the incident are still under investigation. We are therefore not in a position to comment further beyond our published statements.”
“We remain fully committed to supporting the ongoing investigation and are in close coordination with the relevant government authorities and regulators,” the spokesperson added.
President Donald Trump told reporters Thursday that there would be renewed strikes against Iran if it was behind the attack.
“You just ask them,” he said. “They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.”
There are no indications that Iran directed or was involved in the attack, a senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation told NBC News.
Raf Sanchez and Shira Pinson reported from Tel Aviv. Freddie Clayton reported from London. Tom Winter and Jonathan Dienst reported from New York.
Raf Sanchez is a foreign correspondent for NBC News.
Shira Pinson is a London based multimedia producer for NBC News.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.
Tom Winter is NBC’s National Law Enforcement and Intelligence Correspondent.
Jonathan Dienst is chief justice contributor for NBC News and chief investigative reporter for WNBC-TV in New York.

articles.title_orig: Elena Rybakina loses first match as world No. 1 to 118th-ranked opponent
articles.title_zh: Elena Rybakina loses first match as world No. 1 to 118th-ranked opponent
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING – Three-time Grand Slam champion Elena Rybakina crashed out of the China Open with a shock 3-6, 6-4, 6-3 loss to unseeded Alina Charaeva in the second round on Saturday, marking a disappointing start to her reign as world No 1.
The 27-year-old was playing for the first time since defeating four-time major winner Aryna Sabalenka to capture the U.S. Open title last month.
Rybakina had skipped Kazakhstan’s Billie Jean King Cup Finals campaign after what she described as a physically demanding month.
Charaeva, a 24-year-old Russian-born Armenian ranked 118th in the world, etched her name into the record books by becoming the lowest-ranked competitor since the introduction of the WTA rankings in 1975 to rally from a set down to defeat the world’s top-ranked player.
Having weathered Rybakina’s early charge, Charaeva converted five of eight break-point opportunities and won 76% of points behind her first serve. Rybakina struggled on serve, committing seven double faults in the 2-hour, 11-minute contest at the WTA 1000 hardcourt event.
Charaeva will next meet Britain’s Sonay Kartal.
In the men’s draw, German top seed Alexander Zverev swept aside local hope Shang Juncheng 6-0, 6-3 in the round of 16.
Fresh from his U.S. Open triumph and after helping Team Europe win the Laver Cup, Zverev will next take on 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic in Sunday’s quarterfinal.
The 39-year-old Serb boasts a perfect 31-0 record at the ATP 500 event and holds the tournament record with six China Open titles.

articles.title_orig: ‘Dabo (Swinney) Should Be Ashamed,’ ‘He Made This Bed’ — CFB World Shows Clemson HC No Mercy As Tigers Get Mauled in Blowout Loss to No. 4 Miami
articles.title_zh: ‘Dabo (Swinney) Should Be Ashamed,’ ‘He Made This Bed’ — CFB World Shows Clemson HC No Mercy As Tigers Get Mauled in Blowout Loss to No. 4 Miami
articles.content_orig:
There was nowhere for Dabo Swinney to hide as his Clemson Tigers were caged by the Miami Hurricanes in what served as a stark reminder of the current state of the program. The unbeaten No. 4 Miami bullied Clemson all the way to a 41-13 rout at Memorial Stadium.
As the Tigers were left to lick their wounds, criticism of Swinney was swift and pointed, with fans and analysts questioning the direction of a program that had been held up as the gold standard in years past.
The Tigers fell to 3-2 after the deflating loss to the high-flying Hurricanes, and social media quickly turned its attention toward Swinney, Clemson's direction, and whether the longtime coach can get the program back among the sport's elite.
After what was the fourth-worst loss for the Tigers under their head coach, fans were quick to ask a pressing question: Is it time for Swinney to step aside?
"Dabo's mad, but not mad enough," wrote one Clemson fan page . "He made this bed with his roster management. Two games against elite rosters, both ending in lopsided losses. Pretty easy to see why. It's about the Jimmy's & the Joe's."
Another Clemson fan account vented its frustrations, writing , "Honestly, Dabo should be ashamed of what this program has become. I'm tired of his 'We've won a lot' BS. This is a huge falloff.
"To go from one of the top programs in the country to a team that is lucky to get more than two TDs per game is a huge disappointment."
Pack Power 247 editor Cory Smith remarked , "This isn't just a change of the guard in the ACC. This is an absolute [expletive]-whooping with no mercy from Mario Cristobal and Miami for Dabo Swinney and the corpse that remains of the program."
PREDICT THE CFB SEASON: PFN's Free CFB Playoff Predictor
One Clemson reporter chimed in , "The fact that Dabo chose this over getting a QB from the portal just shows me that he doesn't give a [expletive]."
Meanwhile, this fan decided to add some perspective, writing , "I understand Clemson might want to move on from Dabo Swinney, but I hope we all remember he made that program nationally relevant.
"Are we really going to say a coach like Dabo, who led Clemson to two national titles, isn't good enough for the program?"
One Miami analyst kept it simple, writing , "Bye bye, Dabo!"
DIVE IN: PFN's Free CFB HQ — Team and Player Stats, Info, and More
The numbers certainly gave Swinney's critics more than enough ammunition to work with. The Tigers managed just 55 rushing yards on 31 attempts tonight, averaging a mere 1.8 yards per carry against Miami's defense.
Clemson quarterback Tait Reynolds, who ranks #161 in the nation with a PFN QB Impact Score of 60.6, threw for 295 yards, but the Tigers never developed enough balance offensively to consistently threaten the Hurricanes.
Clemson entered the matchup ranked #131 in the nation with a PFN Team Offense Impact Score of 61.0 and a Defense Impact Score of 76.3 (#65).
Then there's the case of the self-inflicted mistakes. Clemson committed 10 penalties for 91 yards, including a costly false start near the Miami goal line on third-and-1.
Swinney's reaction to that misstep quickly went viral and served as a fitting image for how the night unfolded.
Miami was also simply far more explosive and ready to go for the jugular. The Hurricanes averaged 6.8 yards per play compared with Clemson's 4.7, finishing with 419 total yards while repeatedly producing chunk plays.

articles.title_orig: Tennessee Commissioner Resigns After Failed Execution of Christa Pike
articles.title_zh: Tennessee Commissioner Resigns After Failed Execution of Christa Pike
articles.content_orig:
The head of Tennessee’s prison system is resigning, Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday, the first major staff shake-up since Christa Pike ’s stunning failed execution left her unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital.
Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, will step down this month, Lee said. Some of the governor’s fellow Republicans and other elected officials had been urging a change in leadership.
It was the second time since May that Tennessee has not been able to execute a prisoner who was seemingly moments away from death.
The governor also announced that former US Attorney Ed Stanton would lead a review of what happened in Pike’s death chamber. Stanton previously was named to conduct a review after Lee called off a different execution in 2022; he found in that case that Tennessee had not complied with its own lethal injection process.
Strada said in a statement that resigning was “in the best interest of Tennesseans” while Stanton’s review is conducted. The state failed to execute Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug, pentobarbital.
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
There was no immediate response from Pike’s lawyers for an update Saturday on her condition at a hospital. They had disclosed Friday that she was on a ventilator and unconscious in the hours following the execution attempt and that hospital staff were trying to clear the two doses of pentobarbital .
The shocking failure has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted any new executions. Strada said he believes the state “carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol.”
Why botched lethal injections are becoming more common
Pike’s legal team welcomed Strada’s departure but said “it does nothing to help Christa now.”
“What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” the four-lawyer team said. “We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.”
Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
Pike was extraordinarily cooperative with the execution team, even instructing them to “please try here, please try here” as they tried to insert lines, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters Thursday.
In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but couldn’t get a secondary IV line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute him again.
Strada took over the Correction Department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee was changing its lethal injection protocol and would use only pentobarbital.
Four people have been executed in Tennessee since 2025, according to the Correction Department .
Court filings show that Strada’s job included overseeing executions in Arizona when they resumed in 2022 following an eight-year break.
Christa Pike is on a ventilator and unconscious after surviving lethal injection. What happened?
Clarence Dixon was the first that year . The medical team had trouble finding a vein to administer the lethal drugs and finally made an incision in his groin area. The process took about 25 minutes.
That same year in Arizona, medical staff preparing Frank Atwood for execution initially could not locate a vein in his right arm but inserted the IV in his right hand — at Atwood’s suggestion, said Henry Brean, an Arizona Daily Star reporter who was a witness.
Strada announced Murray Hooper’s execution by lethal injection, the third in 2022. There was an unsuccessful attempt to insert an IV line in his right arm. The IV in Hooper’s leg was inserted into his femoral artery.
“When Governor Lee hired Strada to fix execution problems in Tennessee, his problematic history of executions in Arizona was well known,” said Kit Thomas, an attorney who has represented people on Tennessee’s death row.

articles.title_orig: Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban
articles.title_zh: Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban
articles.content_orig:
‘AbortOmat’ in Warsaw offers novel way to challenge country’s restrictions and allow women swift, anonymous access
They call it the “world’s first parcel locker for abortion pills”. Polish campaigners have launched a new means of distribution as part of their ongoing effort to skirt the country’s near-total ban on abortion.
Painted pink and framed by zebra-striped curtains, the 22-compartment “AbortOmat” in Warsaw allows women to access the pills swiftly and anonymously using a six-digit code. The service was envisaged for those who cannot or do not want to wait days for mail delivery due to a missed miscarriage or health complications, or who worry about receiving the pills at home.
“And why not?” said Kinga Jelinska, the director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, the two groups behind last week’s launch.
“You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, whatever and receive it practically the same or next day,” she said. “Why not abortion pills, where in some cases there might be more urgency?”
The innovation comes six years after people across Poland took to the streets to protest against the tightening of abortion laws that already ranked among the strictest in Europe, setting off the country’s largest demonstrations since the fall of communism. In 2023, the protests were credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk, and his promises to overhaul the laws within 100 days, into power.
Since then, political stagnation has set in, said Jelinska, citing comments made last year by Tusk in which the prime minister said there was “simply no majority” to change the laws to allow abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy. Tusk instead hinted that his government was intent on doing things differently, telling reporters that it would not prosecute those who helped to facilitate abortions.
While the possession or ingestion of abortion pills is not outlawed in Poland, provision of the medication or helping someone to obtain it is considered a crime punishable by up to three years in prison.
The locker offers a novel way to challenge these restrictions, said Jelinska. “It’s a little bit of a hack on the law,” she said. “The law is about directly giving to someone. So here we have a machine in between, which makes the legality of everything much more vague.”
The locker sits inside the abortion centre that was opened in March 2025 by the Abortion Dream Team. Described as the first of its kind in democratic Poland, it offers a safe space for people to consult on abortion options or receive support while they take the pill.
after newsletter promotion
Symbolically located across the street from the Polish parliament, the centre has allowed campaigners to shine a spotlight on the continued need for abortion access in Poland while also providing services to a wide array of people, said Jelinska. “It has exceeded our expectations.”
But it had also laid bare how few in power were willing to stand up for them, she said. “The one thing that has surprised us, and it speaks to the political situation, is that there are protests in front of the centre; three, sometimes four times a week.”
While usually less than a dozen people turn up, the protesters regularly use sirens and vuvuzelas to make their point, leaving campaigners worried that the noise levels would eventually result in neighbours asking the centre to relocate. “Neither the city or the police have reacted. So that has been a big disappointment to us,” said Jelinska.
It was a glimpse of how these organisations had increasingly felt abandoned by politicians, even as about 50,000 people in Poland contacted the wider network of pro-choice organisations last year seeking help, said Jelinska. “I think in Poland, abortion access won’t be solved by politics but by women and communities,” she said. “We cannot trust politicians with our own bodies.”

articles.title_orig: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
articles.title_zh: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
articles.content_orig:
The co-pilot who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and successfully take control of the plane.
Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.
Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.
A crash axe is usually kept ​in the cockpit in case of emergencies.
The weapon used has been a key question for investigators, given the stringent security on such a sensitive route. Early reports from passengers on board had suggested it might have been a knife.
The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.
The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times have named him as Hamam al-Hammami. There has been no official confirmation of this.
While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.
Australian authorities confirmed on Sunday they were investigating his "links" to the country, but did not provide any details.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation, citing sources, reported he was issued a student visa in 2014 and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017 before leaving the country.
The ABC said his student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was not enrolled in a course at that time.
Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported.
He then completed a three-year distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK and graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.
Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu said that after the attacker was subdued on the flight, he called out to the crew "Kill me, kill me!"
The Israeli prime minister added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidal… It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."
He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".
The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.
He also said investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.
Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.
The pilot, who is from India, was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday.
"I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again," Machchhar said.
About two and half hours after the plane took off from Dubai International Airport it begun to plunge sharply.
The plane signalled a "general emergency" code, squawk 7700, before switching to squawk 7500, a code reporting "unlawful interference", or hijacking.
In an interview with the BBC, one passenger described the moment he realised that something was wrong.
Almog Itali said: "Suddenly the aeroplane started to, like a rollercoaster, to drop down [with] a massive G-force. It was falling down for 20 or 30 seconds, rapidly, and then balanced, and then started once again to fall down."
People then began to rush to the cockpit, he said.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said on Thursday that the alarm was raised onboard by an Israeli woman, Tali Manes, who heard a commotion coming from the cockpit.
Her husband, Zvika, along with three other men - Yaniv Hayun, Dr Shota Musayev and Asaf Rajuan - entered the cockpit after Capt Machchhar managed to open the door despite his injuries.
Hayun said, in a video released by the prime minister's office, that the attacker was "trying to destroy the instruments in order to disable the plane".
Hayun then described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him outside the cockpit before other passengers helped to pin him down.
He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane. "The plane started to level out, a bit more, and then [another] pilot told me he was taking control from there," he said.
In an interview with CNN on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu said the stabbed pilot, passengers and second crew had "managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster".

articles.title_orig: The Draw is Done! The Baku World Championships is Only Hours Away...
articles.title_zh: The Draw is Done! The Baku World Championships is Only Hours Away...
articles.content_orig:
Ahead of the first contests, due to commence at 11:30am at the National Gymnastics Arena on Sunday, there are still final preparations to be made; those of the delegations as well as the organisers. For athletes and coaches, it is imperative to have concrete information about the draw, opponents and running order. Therefore, on the eve of the competition, the draw has been held in the presence of officials from the International Judo Federation and the Azerbaijan Judo Federation.
Present for the IJF were Secretary General Dr Lisa Allan, Head Sport Director Mr Vladimir Barta and Head Referee Director Mr Juan Carlos Barcos.
Present for the Azerbaijan Judo Federation were AJF Executive Vice President Mr Rashad Rasullu, Head of the Sports Department of the Ministry of Youth and Sports Mr Elnur Mammadov and AJF Vice President Mr Elnur Mammadli
Dr Lisa Allan led the introductions and formal welcome on behalf of the International Judo Federation and IJF President Mr Marius Vizer, “Dear judo family, it is a great pleasure and honour to welcome you all to Baku. This is a city with a proud sporting tradition and it is a pleasure to be here once again alongside our friends and colleagues from the Azerbaijan Judo Federation, Secretary General Rasullu and his team.
On behalf of International Judo Federation President Mr Marius Vizer and the entire IJF, we are delighted to welcome you to the IJF World Championships for Seniors, Individuals and Mixed Teams.
We would like to express our sincere appreciation to President Nabiyev and everyone at the Azerbaijan Judo Federation for their continued commitment to judo and for the passion, professionalism and dedication they demonstrate consistently in the hosting of IJF World Judo Tour events in Azerbaijan. Once again, this championship brings together our worldwide judo family, united by the same spirit, the same values and, above all, our shared love of judo."
"Over the next eight days, we will have the privilege of witnessing the world’s finest judoka compete at the highest level. Here at the National Gymnastics Arena and with fans watching around the world through JudoTV, our live streaming platform, we look forward to experiencing moments of excellence, determination and unforgettable competition.
We also extend our heartfelt thanks to all our member national federations, partners and sponsors. Your continued trust, commitment and support are essential to the growth and development of our sport.
Finally, we wish all athletes and delegations every success for the championships. May these days in Baku be filled with great judo, memorable moments and a wonderful celebration of our sport. Welcome to Baku and welcome to the IJF World Judo Championships; thank you.”
Mr Rashad Rasullu then took the floor, “Dear Dr Allan. Mr Barta, Mr Barcos, dear judo family, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon and welcome to Baku! It is a great honour for Azerbaijan to host the World Judo Championships once again and to welcome the international judo family to our capital."
"The development of sport in Azerbaijan has always received strong attention and support at the highest level. Under the leadership of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, His Excellency Ilham Aliyev, significant effort has been made to develop modern sport infrastructure, support our athletes and host major international sporting events in our country.
In the coming days, Baku will bring together the world's leading judoka for one of the most important events on the international judo calendar. We are proud to provide a stage where athletes from around the world can compete at the highest level in the spirit of respect and fair play.
On behalf of the Azerbaijan Judo Federation, I would like to express our sincere gratitude to International Judo Federation President Mr Marius Vizer and Minister of Youth and Sports of the Republic of Azerbaijan Mr Farid Gayibov for their valuable support and contribution to the organisation of the World Championships. I would also like to thank the International Judo Federation, the Ministry of Youth and Sports of Azerbaijan, our sponsors and everyone involved in the preparation and organisation of the championships."
"Today's draw marks the final step before the competition begins. I wish all athletes good health, successful performances and the very best of luck on the tatami. We hope you enjoy your time in Baku and the hospitality of Azerbaijan. I wish everyone a successful and memorable world championships. Thank you!”
Head of the Sports Department of the Ministry of Youth and Sports Mr Elnur Mammadov then spoke proudly, “Dear International Judo Federation, dear guests, for second time, Azerbaijan is hosting a world championships. We are delighted to welcome you to this prestigious event, being held at the highest standard. The reason for this is the great contribution from the IJF.
Today President Ilham Aliyev awarded the special Order of Friendship to President Vizer for his fruitful efforts and contribution to judo here and around the world. Judo is one of most popular sports in Azerbaijan and our results show this.
I thank the Azerbaijan Judo Federation for all their hard work. The competition starts tomorrow and I’m sure the spectators will enjoy seeing these 600 athletes compete. I wish you all good luck.”
Next there were some words about refereeing matters from Mr Barcos, “Dear judo family, the IJF Refereeing Commission has selected the best possible group of referees, to achieve the best results here in Baku.” He then clarified the contest review process for coaches, to ensure correct processes are followed.
To conduct the mechanics of the draw, IJF Head Sport Director Mr Vladimir Barta took the floor, supported by the IJF IT Team.“Distinguished guests, dear judo family, we begin the draw of the World Judo Championships 2026. We have 93 countries and a total of 623 athletes present. The largest group is the men’s -100 kg category with 56 entrants.”
Mr Barta’s introduction was followed by a video breakdown of the top names in each category and the live draw. When the draw for the individual competition was concluded, focus moved to the mixed team competition which was also drawn, as was the starting category for the first round: +70 kg.
As the final preparations are concluded, the excitement continues to rise. Tune into JudoTV to catch all the action as it unfolds.

articles.title_orig: Health Policy Watch | COVID-19 drops out of world’s top 10 causes of death for first time since pandemic began
articles.title_zh: Health Policy Watch | COVID-19 drops out of world’s top 10 causes of death for first time since pandemic began
articles.content_orig:
COVID-19 dropped out of the world’s 10 leading causes of death in 2023 for the first time since the pandemic began in 2020, and only two years after it topped the list, according to new World Health Organization estimates released Friday (2 October).
The virus directly killed an estimated 0.9 million people in 2023, ranking 14th, as global life expectancy climbed back to near its pre-pandemic level. WHO declared an end to COVID-19 as a global health emergency in May that year.
Revised figures now rank COVID-19 as the world’s leading cause of death in 2021, with 9.4 million direct deaths. WHO’s earlier estimates had placed it second that year. Together with 5.3 million deaths in 2020, the new figures put the virus’s direct toll in the first two years of the pandemic at 14.7 million.

articles.title_orig: AI Deal Frenzy Powers Hong Kong Fundraising to Record Summer
articles.title_zh: AI Deal Frenzy Powers Hong Kong Fundraising to Record Summer
articles.content_orig:
Summer break? Not this year. Hong Kong bankers stayed on the field as AI-fueled capital raises set a third-quarter record, with $47.5 billion coming from IPOs, placements and block trades. The surge has pushed total proceeds so far this year past $92 billion, close to the all-time high of $112.5 billion set in 2021. Rising bond yields and choppy deal outcomes, though, are making both issuers and investors a bit more guarded.
Artificial intelligence didn't just nudge the market back to life - it hit fast forward. Chinese companies are tapping larger checks and returning to the market sooner to bankroll growth in the fast-growing sector.
The headline print: Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. raised $10.2 billion in a follow-on, the period's largest deal. Zhongji Innolight Co. hauled in almost $8 billion in Hong Kong 's biggest listing in nearly seven years. And AI model developer Z.AI Co. amassed $9.6 billion this year via its IPO, subsequent share sales, and convertible bond issues.
Others wasted no time after lockups expired. In a feverish July, model maker MiniMax Group Inc. plus chipmakers Shanghai Iluvatar CoreX Semiconductor Co. and Shanghai Biren Technology Co. returned to the market soon after their IPO lockups ended.
Capital raising tells you where the smart money thinks the next cycle is heading. Market Briefs tracks the deal flow free every morning .
Momentum extended across Asia-Pacific, with equity issuance surpassing $120 billion during the third quarter, marking the region's strongest third-quarter in six years. Some of the heftiest deals came out of Mainland China, highlighted by a 66.6 billion yuan ($9.9 billion) IPO by memory chipmaker CXMT Corp., the country's second-largest on record.
India snapped back too. Since July, equity offerings there raised a record $26 billion, marking the country's strongest quarter. Highlights included a $3.2 billion government stake sale in Life Insurance Corp., plus the much-anticipated $2.4 billion IPO of National Stock Exchange of India Ltd., which ranks as the country's second-largest on record.
All this fundraising arrived against a shakier market tape. The MSCI Asia-Pacific Index dropped by as much as 7% in July, and Hong Kong 's Hang Seng Tech Index has been trending lower this year. Deal quality is under the microscope: of the 10 largest Hong Kong offerings since the start of July, only two are trading above water. "So as we go into year-end, I would expect that investors potentially become more selective about where they put their money to work."
Even so, the pipeline is substantial. The Philippines is set for a milestone: Mynt Inc., owner of the GCash app, has priced what's poised to be the country's largest-ever IPO. Australia is set to partake in the AI wave too, with a forthcoming $5 billion IPO by data center operator Firmus Grid Ltd., expected to be among the country's largest listings ever. And as Goldman's Wang put it: "Investors will be more selective.
More deals are coming, even as markets wobble. That means plenty of choice, but also wider spreads in outcomes as investors zero in on quality and steer clear of anything that can't clear the bar on growth, profitability or both. Watch the mix: AI-linked names are fueling supply, while rate jitters and soft first-day pops are testing demand. How those two forces settle will shape where fresh capital actually sticks.
A record quarter in Asia says the AI trade is far from a US-only story. Get the free Market Briefs daily newsletter and follow the money .

articles.title_orig: Why Trump should welcome China's help to end the Iran war
articles.title_zh: Why Trump should welcome China's help to end the Iran war
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
NEW YORK — President Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran  if it fails to negotiate a deal over its nuclear program, delivering a defensive speech justifying the mission at the United Nations on Tuesday.
His remarks come more than six months into a war that has grown increasingly unpopular at home, with fewer than a third of Americans approving of the president’s handling of the conflict, according to recent polls.
“I have a big decision to make,” he told world leaders gathered at the U.N. General Assembly in New York, with Iranian diplomats in attendance.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before — maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy again?
“Do I drive them into hell,” he continued, “with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness?”
The war has carried steep political costs for the president and his party ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November, increasing inflation and energy prices due to disruptions in commercial shipping traffic through key waterways in the Middle East.
Defense officials say the conflict has also placed a huge burden on U.S. munitions stockpiles, as Iran continues firing ballistic missiles and drones at American assets and bases throughout the region.
But Trump denied that the war has depleted U.S. stocks. “That’s not true,” he said.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election,” Trump said. “We must be equally united in maintaining pressure.”
The rise in global gas prices has sparked protests around the world. But Trump’s vow to ensure Tehran never acquires a nuclear weapon — an issue that for decades united the international community — generated applause throughout the chamber.
The president’s actions stand to color the backdrop of a week that will feature meetings with world leaders at the U.N. and a state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Launching  the war on Iran in February, Trump projected the campaign would last roughly six weeks, with the stated objective of disabling Iran’s ballistic missile program, its navy and its nuclear infrastructure. He also vowed a day would soon come when the Iranian people could rise up against their government and reclaim their country.
More than six months later, the Islamic Republic stands. Iran’s ballistic missiles continue to test U.S. air defenses across the Middle East, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains depressed, and talks over the future of Iran’s nuclear program have collapsed.
Explaining his decision to start the war, Trump said that he decided not to let the problem of Iran’s nuclear work “fester,” and warned that its ballistic missile program was being designed as a shield to protect its nuclear program from foreign attack.
“Iran’s goal was to complete their mad dash to a nuclear bomb from behind this conventional ballistic missile shield,” Trump said. “They were the bully of the Middle East, but they’re the bully no more.”
He said the United States has repeatedly offered Iran a deal  that would open up economic cooperation between the two nations in exchange for an end to  Iran’s nuclear work. “They absolutely refused,” he added. “That was a big mistake.”
U.S. and Iranian officials met on the sidelines of the annual general assembly, in a meeting Trump later described as productive.
“Very good meeting,” he told reporters traveling with him in New York. “I can’t imagine why they wouldn’t want to. It’s greatness, potential greatness, or obliteration.”
When outlining his priorities on the Western Hemisphere, Trump vowed to use “unmatched military might” when necessary if drug cartel activity in other countries poses a threat to the United States.
“Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,” Trump said.
Trump said his administration is reasserting its power over regional drug cartels, which he characterized as “the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere.” He said drug cartel members should be “killed, exiled  or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release,” and said Mexico was the “epicenter of the cartel violence.”
“Mexico must reclaim control of its soil from the enemies of humanity,” he said.
In the same remarks, Trump said his administration is seeking a “fundamental change” in Cuba, which he called a “failed state.” He said talks on what comes next for the communist island are being negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
“It will fall,” he said, as members of the Cuban delegation walked out of the room.
Also in the room was Delcy Rodríguez, the acting president of Venezuela. She has worked closely with the Trump administration since the U.S. military captured Nicolás Maduro and brought him to the United States to face drug trafficking charges.
Rodríguez and Trump were expected to have a “pull aside” meeting, said Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. Their encounter is the first time the two leaders met in person since Maduro’s capture.
Because Rodríguez is a holdover from the Maduro government, the meeting has drawn criticism in Venezuela, where many believe Trump is legitimizing her. Earlier this month, those tensions grew when the U.S. government entered an agreement with an oil producer to develop Venezuelan’s vast oil resources, with Rodríguez’s blessing.
The sweeping oil deal raised uncertainty about how entrenched the unelected government may become, more so after Trump said he did not think Venezuela was ready to hold democratic elections yet.
“It’s very new. We took them out of a dictatorship and we’re getting along great with the government,” Trump told reporters earlier this month. But he said an election would happen “soon.”
Also Tuesday, after months of threatening to seize Greenland , Trump signed a security agreement with the leaders of the Arctic territory and Denmark, one that he lauded as “tremendous for Europe and the United States.”
Details of the deal remained vague upon its signing. But Trump told the General Assembly that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all of the needs” of the Danish territory.
“We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe and other places,” Trump said.
The agreement would bar any U.S. adversaries from establishing a military presence in Greenland.
Mette Frederiksen, the Danish prime minister, on Tuesday said the accord “respects the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark as well as Greenland’s right to self-determination.”
Action is still needed by the Danish and Greenland governments before it can be enforced, though Trump characterized it as more immediate. He told the General Assembly that the United States planned to immediately grow its military presence in the Arctic island. The agreement says Denmark and Greenland will review U.S. requests to expand the military presence under “accelerated governmental approval procedures.”
“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” he said. “We will be building two major military bases.”
Frederiksen told Trump on Tuesday that the deal would help protect the United States from foreign adversaries.
“Mr. President, you’ve been very clear you don’t want adversaries to come too close. I fully agree. And with this deal, they are not,” she said. “We are making sure that they will not be allowed to get any control or significant influence in Greenland.”
Wilner reported from New York and Ceballos from Washington.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Coast Guard locates debris from missing plane off Nantucket, search for missing passengers ongoing
articles.title_zh: U.S. Coast Guard locates debris from missing plane off Nantucket, search for missing passengers ongoing
articles.content_orig:
The Coast Guard located debris that was confirmed to be associated with the missing aircraft off Nantucket, the U.S. Coast Guard told NewsCenter 5 on Saturday.
The search is still ongoing for the six missing passengers who were on board, the Coast Guard said.
The Gulfstream G-100 aircraft departed L.F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda and was traveling to Boston's Logan International Airport.
A Massport spokesperson confirmed that the aircraft did not arrive at Logan Airport as scheduled.
The Bermuda government said it has been in contact with the families of those on board.
“My thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time," said Premier David Burt. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”
In a statement from Skyport, the company that manages Wade International Airport, a spokesperson said that the aircraft was a Canadian-registered air ambulance that left its airport for Boston at 12:41 a.m. on Saturday.
The company said there were four crew members and two passengers on board. The passengers were traveling to Boston for medical care.
"The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has advised that air traffic controllers subsequently lost contact with the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, and a search is currently underway," the spokesperson said. "Skyport has no further information to provide at this time."
The Federal Aviation Administration said it issued a search and rescue alert for the plane at 1:20 a.m.
The FAA notified the U.S. Coast Guard that it lost contact with the plane, which is registered to Canadian-based Latitude Air Ambulance. The company confirmed that the missing plane is among its fleet. The Coast Guard's response includes crews from Air Station Cape Cod, a 47-foot motor lifeboat crew from Station Brant Point and the USCGC William Sparling -- a fast response cutter.
The search is about 13 nautical miles off the coast and extends from about 30 nautical miles wide and 20 nautical miles long, according to the Coast Guard.
WCVB will have more information when it becomes available.

articles.title_orig: Cornell president calls alleged gang rape ‘deeply disturbing,’ pledges greater transparency
articles.title_zh: Cornell president calls alleged gang rape ‘deeply disturbing,’ pledges greater transparency
articles.content_orig:
Immediately after Katiana Soenen says she was sexually assaulted as a freshman at Brown University in 2021, she struggled to understand what had happened and questioned her own actions.
“I spent the first kind of like two hours after really trying to figure out if I had done something wrong or what I might have done to have caused it,” Soenen said.
A friend picked her up from the house where she says it happened and drove her back to her dorm. A few hours later, Soenen called him and described the encounter, saying the experience did not feel right.
He responded: “Katiana, I don’t think that was consensual.”
Hearing that from someone else helped her solidify her understanding of the encounter.
“It wasn’t really until he told me that that it hit me: This wasn’t a consensual experience.”
When Soenen learned about the alleged gang rape of former Cornell student Jane Doe at a fraternity house in 2024, she says she immediately saw parallels between herself and the anonymous student, particularly in her progression from denial and shame to acceptance and reporting.
“I saw a lot of myself in Jane Doe,” she said.
As new information emerging this week raises questions over how the Cornell case was handled by the university and law enforcement, national outrage and demands for accountability have also reignited the conversation around sexual assault on college campuses .
In the three weeks between when the former Cornell student was allegedly gang raped and when she described the night to campus police, Doe appeared to wrestle with shame and her stance had evolved on whether an assault took place, according to records obtained exclusively by the New York Times and corroborated by Doe’s attorney.
In an article published Thursday, the Times cited documents from the university’s formal Title IX investigation that shed new light on how Doe initially viewed the night’s events, discussed them with her roommates and communicated with some of the men before she went to university police.
Doe’s attorney, Thomas P. Giuffra, told CNN her reaction represented a “textbook reaction to trauma.”
“Ms. Doe’s internal processing went from denial, to shame and ultimately acceptance that she had been raped by people that she thought were her friends,” Giuffra told CNN on Thursday.
Experts told CNN Soenen’s and Doe’s accounts aren’t unique . While every sexual assault survivor processes their trauma differently, denial, guilt, self-blame and shame are common. Both Doe and Soenen ultimately reported their alleged assaults to their universities before filing civil lawsuits criticizing the institutions’ responses.
After Soenen was allegedly sexually assaulted at an off-campus residence in May 2021, she says she initially tried to reinterpret the experience as consensual before speaking with her friend.
“I kept being eaten alive by this idea of if he did this to me, he’s capable of doing this again to somebody else,” she recounted.
Soenen says she reported the alleged assault to the university about a week later.
Initially, she believed Brown’s systems would protect and support her. But as the process continued, she says she lost confidence in their response, calling it a “secondary violation.”
“I quickly began to lose that hope,” she said.
Brown has argued the alleged assault was outside Title IX’s scope since it occurred off campus and maintained that staff responded appropriately. CNN has reached out to Brown University for further comment.
Brown discussed options with Soenen, including academic accommodations, counseling, a no-contact order and formal complaint procedures, according to court documents. She ultimately did not file a formal complaint, alleging she was discouraged by the university, which Brown has denied, the documents said.
The second time, her denial was even more pronounced.
About a month after the incident, Soenen said she was assaulted again at an off-campus party while heavily intoxicated. She said she could not confidently identify her assailant, though others witnessed part of the incident and intervened, she told CNN.
Soenen described feeling “so dirty,” wanting to remove any physical reminders and pretend it didn’t happen.
“I really tried to almost convince myself that it hadn’t happened, that it was like a bad dream or something.”
In the Cornell case, Doe told her roommates she had taken ketamine and had sex with multiple men but did not use the words “rape” or “assault,” the Times reported, citing Title IX files.
One roommate said Doe appeared to be “in shock” and was “not really understanding the gravity of what she was saying.” Her sorority sister reportedly told investigators Doe “had not yet processed what had happened” when they met a day later.
After one of the men apologized and said he felt terrible and was too under the influence of drugs and alcohol to “shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand,” Doe reassured him that “non of the sexual stuff was illegal,” the Times reported.
Cornell’s investigation found she considered returning to the fraternity house for a Halloween party, according to two sources familiar with the school’s Title IX investigation. Her attorney described that as part of her denial.
Experts describe denial as a protective response: Survivors may be in shock, have incomplete or nonlinear memories, blame themselves, delay reporting or avoid calling what happened to them an assault.
Dr. Rose Olson, a physician and researcher at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, says those trauma responses “should not be used as evidence of fault.” Reactions can include crying, anger, shock, numbness, calmness or even laughter, she said.
Megan Cutter, chief of victim services at RAINN, said survivors commonly call RAINN’s National Sexual Assault Hotline, saying, “I think something happened” or “I’m not sure what happened.” They may initially describe what happened as a bad decision or experience they disliked because using terms like “rape” or “assault” can make the trauma feel more real.
It could be attributed to the fawn stress response, in which a survivor may appease or try to maintain peace with the person who harmed them, Cutter said.
Survivors also often “test the waters” by initially disclosing only part of an experience, and the kind of response they receive can shape whether they seek help, said Laura Palumbo, communications director at the National Sexual Violence Resource Center.
Research into the neurobiology of trauma shows that partial memories are normal because the brain may struggle to process information during a traumatic experience, Palumbo said.
Kim Villanueva, president of the National Organization for Women, emphasized, “It’s not up to the survivor to tell the perfect story in perfect order.”
Because, she says, she had been assaulted twice in a short period, Soenen felt ashamed to ask for help.
“I thought that clearly something must have been wrong with me if it had happened to me twice,” she said. “I was almost embarrassed to even call for help because I felt like that was a stain on my character.”
Soenen also wondered whether saying no differently or more forcefully could have prevented the assault.
“If I had said no one more time, maybe it wouldn’t have happened,” she said.
Soenen considered getting a sexual assault forensic exam but says she was overwhelmed and didn’t understand how the process worked. She worried about who would pay for it, whether it would appear on her insurance and if it would be a repeat of her first report.
“Why is anything different going to happen the second time?” she thought.
After her experiences, Soenen said she rarely left her dorm because she was afraid of encountering the people she says assaulted her.
“Every man who somewhat fit the little bits and details that I remembered, I wondered if it was him,” she said.
For Doe, the documents reportedly detail how rumors about the alleged gang rape led her to fear reputational damage and left her humiliated.

articles.title_orig: Bernie Sanders makes a late push for California billionaire tax
articles.title_zh: Bernie Sanders makes a late push for California billionaire tax
articles.content_orig:
Google cofounder Sergey Brin has now spent more than nine figures combating California’s proposed wealth tax.
According to filings , Brin donated a total of $102 million to the group Building a Better California, a PAC and political advocacy organization opposing the state’s billionaire tax and supporting other pro-business policies and housing and infrastructure affordability. Campaign filings show efforts to block this tax have exceeding $187 million, making Brin the largest sole contributor to the effort. Contributions supporting the bill have meanwhile reached about $32 million.
Proposition 40 , which will be on the ballot in November, would impose a one-time, 5% tax on California’s 200 billionaires, with 90% of the revenue from the proposed measure going toward the state’s health care program and 10% going toward education, food assistance, and administration. Brin, with a net worth of nearly $260 billion , could owe about $13 billion as a result of the tax.
California, the most populous state, has become the epicenter of the conversation around the K-shaped economy, or the diverging fortunes of those with wealth and those without it. While the Golden State has a $4 trillion GDP, making its economy about the same size as the United Kingdom’s, it also has 18% of its residents living below the poverty line , the highest in the country, in part because of its high cost of living.
The ballot measure has caused an uproar among some of California’s wealthiest individuals such as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and PayPal cofounder Peter Thiel, both of whom have donated to organizations against the measure. Brin compared the proposal to his socialist Soviet upbringing.
“I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and know the devastating, oppressive society it created in the Soviet Union. I don’t want California to end up in the same place,” he told the New York Times in a statement in April.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom has joined these tech billionaires in combating the measure, arguing the tax would hurt the state by eroding its tax base, ultimately reducing key revenue for social services.
“The fact is it actually will reduce investments in education,” Newsom said in a Bloomberg Businessweek interview earlier this year. “It will reduce investments in teachers and librarians, childcare. It will reduce investments in firefighting and police.”
The opposition to Prop 40 may, in some ways, be a self-fulfilling prophecy, as billionaires including Brin shift business entities out of California in favor of states without similar wealth taxes. Brin now lists Nevada as his residence, according to state records. Larry Page, who cofounded Google alongside Brin, has converted several of his assets out of California, including Koop, his family office, which was incorporated in Delaware in December 2025. Oceankind, an ocean science nonprofit founded by Page’s wife, Lucy Southworth, in 2018 , was similarly incorporated in Delaware around the same time. Brin, for his own part, reportedly bought a $51 million home near Miami Beach in March.
There’s not yet clear evidence to indicate these billionaires’ anxieties about the future of California are well-founded. On one hand, the six billionaires expected to leave California—Brin, Page, Thiel, as well as car loan magnate Don Hankey, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, and director Steven Spielberg—would have collectively generated about $27 billion in tax revenue, about one-fourth of the $100 billion the proposal is expected to raise through taxes over five years.
On the other hand, billionaires were already paying so little in California income tax their departure may not pack as much of a punch as anticipated. A working paper published by the National Bureau of Economic Research in May noted billionaires residing in the state paid $4.1 billion in income tax last year, about 0.2% of their collective $2 trillion net worth, meaning that even if every billionaire were to leave the state, it would take about 25 years for lost income tax revenue to cancel out the $100 billion sum California is projected to get from the tax. Even if a billionaire mass exodus included one-quarter of the state’s wealthiest residents, it would take a century to equal the $100 billion windfall.
“The proposed one-off California billionaire tax of 5%, payable over five years, is both small relative to California billionaires’ wealth gains and large relative to the taxes they currently pay,” the authors wrote.
A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Aug. 11, 2026.

“Today’s sold-out crowd at the NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals is another tremendous showcase of the passion and enthusiasm St. Louis fans have for NHRA drag racing,” said NHRA President Glen Cromwell. “The team at World Wide Technology Raceway continues to provide an outstanding experience, and it’s exciting to see another packed house in St. Louis during our 75th anniversary season.”
Saturday’s capacity crowd represents NHRA’s 11th sellout of the 2026 season and its third consecutive Saturday sellout during the NHRA Mission Foods Drag Racing Series Countdown to the Championship.
The NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals marks the midpoint of the six-race Countdown playoffs, making every qualifying position and championship bonus point increasingly important. The sold-out Saturday crowd watched two qualifying sessions featuring the stars of Top Fuel, Funny Car, Pro Stock and Pro Stock Motorcycle.

articles.title_orig: Trump defends data centers in Ohio, warns they’ll go to China if US turns them away
articles.title_zh: Trump defends data centers in Ohio, warns they’ll go to China if US turns them away
articles.content_orig:
President Trump defended the rapid buildout of massive data centers Saturday as he rallied supporters in Ohio to turn out for Republican candidates in next month’s midterm elections — warning that blocking the tech projects would hand an advantage to China.
“There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” Trump told supporters at the campaign rally outside Dayton — where he urged voters to back Republican Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.
Trump repeatedly told the crowd in the battleground state to act as though he himself were on the ballot in the November 3 midterms.
“Please pretend that I’m on the ballot, and you need to turn out for a midterm victory,” he said.
Trump said his administration was taking “historic action” to make sure large technology companies behind data centers benefit surrounding communities.
The president tied the data center boom to the global race over artificial intelligence, saying the US was ahead of China in what he repeatedly called “superintelligence.”
Trump said China “doesn’t want to see us,” adding, “We’re beating China” in the technology race as he argued against turning data centers away from the US.
At the same time, Trump backed legislation pushed by Husted that he said would “stop data centers from raising electricity costs and require them to pay their own way.”
Trump said nearly every Senate Democrat had voted days earlier to block the measure.
He vowed to sign the Ratepayer Protection Act “into law immediately within 24 hours” if Republicans prevailed.
The surge in data center development has triggered a bipartisan backlash across the country as communities grapple with the enormous amounts of electricity, water and land required to power the facilities.
The biggest fight has centered on who should pay for the infrastructure needed to serve the projects.
Utilities may need to build new power plants, substations and transmission lines for massive data center loads, raising concerns that households and other businesses could be stuck with higher bills if those costs are spread across the broader rate base.
Water use, noise and sprawling footprints have also fueled resistance, particularly in areas where projects sit near homes or rely on strained water supplies.
Critics have also questioned generous state and local tax breaks for facilities that can cost billions of dollars to build but employ relatively few workers once construction is finished.
The political pressure has prompted officials in several states to rethink the incentives and fast-track approvals once used to lure the industry.
Some states have paused tax breaks or permitting, while others have pushed special utility rates and requirements aimed at making developers shoulder more of the cost of serving their facilities.
Trump was in Ohio after stops in Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama this week as part of what he says will be a 32-day jaunt ahead of the midterms.

articles.content_orig:
Outsourcing life’s mundane tasks buys us freedom, but risks relinquishing the experience of living, says online observer
From cooking and attending hospital visits to doing the actual quarrelling, paid “life stand-ins” are stepping in to manage these tasks, along with errands and awkward moments that many young Chinese would rather avoid.
This trend, known as the “stand-in economy,” is gaining traction among time-strapped consumers who are willing to pay for convenience when daily responsibilities exceed their time, patience, or expertise.
First widely reported by mainland media in 2024, the movement has since blossomed into a vast market for highly personalised errand services.
On RedNote, posts about paid handicraft and assembly assistance have garnered over 120 million views. For example, some users buy intricate Lego sets but lack the time needed to assemble them, opting instead to hire professional builders.

articles.title_orig: France’s violent student protests raise warning for America: ‘A cautionary tale’
articles.title_zh: France’s violent student protests raise warning for America: ‘A cautionary tale’
articles.content_orig:
‘The Big Weekend Show’ panel discusses protests in France over complaints about teacher shortages, school days and deteriorating facilities.
France’s violent student protests are fueling fresh warnings about the consequences of open-border immigration policies, with the unrest being held up as a "cautionary tale" for the U.S.
"I would also say as we’re sitting here in beautiful New York City, this is a cautionary tale," "The Big Weekend Show" co-host Tomi Lahren said Saturday.
She continued: "This is something we’re learning from Europe, and we would be wise to learn from Europe. They decided they wanted to have open borders. They decided they wanted diversity as their strength, and of course, Joe Biden tried that for four years. We’re undoing that currently."
FRANCE'S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT
Policemen stand in front of burning garbage as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools in Paris on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)
Lahren posited that "when you let so many people come into your country, leech off of your system, then the people who are from there are going to at some point get upset."
She said that anger often becomes misplaced and, "they end up lighting things on fire, which I think is stupid no matter what you’re angry with, but it’s no doubt these countries that say we’re going to be a global home for everybody, they end up paying the price, and it’s usually the native Frenchmen, or whenever they are that end up paying the highest price."
Students in Paris began to protest late last month against what they deemed as overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, long school days and deteriorating conditions, blaming the government for not investing enough in education.
REPUBLICAN GLEE ERUPTS AS WHITE HOUSE BOASTS SHARP DECLINE IN IMMIGRATION FROM MUSLIM-MAJORITY NATIONS
A student kicks a tear gas canister during a protest against under-resourced schools in Paris on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)
The demonstrations started peacefully in Paris’ poorer suburbs but quickly spread to Paris itself, then went nationwide in cities like Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours, Nantes, Toulouse ​and Lille, becoming increasingly violent as they expanded.
The protests were also fueled by the government’s 2027 budget unveiling on Thursday, which showed education spending would rise by only 1.7%, excluding teacher pensions, an increase which is below the rate of inflation, Reuters reported.
Rioters have committed arson, vandalism, thrown objects at police and even assaulted people in some cases, prompting authorities to respond with tear gas and rubber bullets.
TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS
Students block the entrance of Voltaire high school in Paris as they protest against under-resourced schools on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)
More than 5,000 protesters were arrested this week across the country, according to Reuters, and more than 400 schools remained closed as of Friday.
Euronews reported Friday that at least 65 school staff members, including 40 principals, have been injured since the unrest began, along with roughly 170 students.
More than 100 high schools have suffered what Education Minister Édouard Geffray described as "severe damage."
French intelligence agencies told a government crisis meeting Thursday that the protest movement had been initiated by politicians from the hard-left France Unbowed Party, known as LFI, Reuters reported Friday.
LIZ PEEK: ANGRY, AFFLUENT AND ADRIFT — WHAT'S DRIVING SOME YOUNG AMERICANS TO VIOLENCE
Anti-riot police officers face protesting students carrying out blockading action outside the secondary school Le Corbusier, in Aubervilliers, northern Paris on Friday. (Lou Benoist / AFP via Getty Images)
LFI has denied the allegations and accused President Emmanuel Macron 's government of politicizing the protests ahead of France's 2027 presidential election.
Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the unrest began with legitimate concerns but has since evolved into something far more serious.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The students’ grievances about missing teachers and deteriorating schools were real at first," Rodan-Benzaquen said. "But dousing a principal in gasoline and attacking firefighters are acts of extreme violence. What makes this politically significant is the effort to turn frustration over schools into a much broader confrontation with the government."
Fox News' Efrat Lachter contributed to this report.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Trump announces $90 payments for seniors on Medicare ahead of midterm elections for premium costs
articles.title_zh: Trump announces $90 payments for seniors on Medicare ahead of midterm elections for premium costs
articles.content_orig:
Fox News co-host Tomi Lahren discusses President Donald Trump's work in his second term and how he handles the media on 'The Evening Edit.'
President Donald Trump announced Friday that his administration would begin sending checks of nearly $100 to more than 20 million seniors to help offset the cost of Medicare Part B premiums.
Trump said in a Truth Social post that the funds — which, based on the figures he provided, would total roughly $2 billion — would come from the Medicare Improvement Fund.
"I am pleased to announce that my Administration will, immediately, begin sending 'Checks' of nearly $100 to over 20 MILLION wonderful Seniors to help pay for their Medicare Part B premiums, which we have already reduced by significant amounts," Trump wrote.
"This money will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, a pointless 'Slush Fund' that has only been used by Dumocrats in Congress to pay for the Waste, Fraud, and Abuse for their Special Interest friends, and drive up Healthcare costs ."
TRUMP SAYS US CAN 'EASILY' AFFORD $1.2T PRICE TAG FOR $5K DIVIDEND TO ADULTS
President Donald Trump announced that more than 20 million Medicare enrollees will receive one-time $90 payments to help cover their Medicare Part B premiums. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
A White House fact sheet said the payments will be $90 per person and will go to more than 20 million Medicare Part B enrollees, with most eligible recipients receiving the money by direct deposit in early October and others getting a mailed check.
The administration said most Part B enrollees qualify, except those whose premiums are already paid by Medicaid or who pay an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount.
In 2026, the standard Medicare Part B monthly premium is $202.90, while the annual deductible is $283, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
Trump said the checks are intended to make Medicare more affordable for seniors.
TRUMP'S INVESTMENT PUSH HITS EUROPE AS IRISH PM EYES NEXT TARIFF BREAK
President Donald Trump speaks during a rally at the Choctaw Event Center in Durant, Okla., Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. (Reuters / Reuters)
"We are finally using this Fund, along with my Most Favored Nations Deals, to substantially LOWER costs for our Seniors," Trump said. "I pledged to protect and preserve Medicare and Social Security, which were on the verge of RUIN by Joe Biden, who foolishly and maliciously let tens of millions of Illegal Aliens into our Country, and we are doing just that for America’s Seniors."
The president said the latest "give back" proposal is separate from another initiative recently unveiled by the Trump administration to issue refund checks to roughly 1 million Americans it says were overcharged for ObamaCare.
An administration official previously told Fox News Digital that the U.S. Treasury had begun issuing $500 refund checks to more than 950,000 Americans across 30 states. Each refund also comes with a letter from Trump.
Trump also said the new Medicare checks would not interfere with his campaign promise to offer a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the upcoming midterm elections .
Trump previously announced the proposed payments, which could potentially cost more than $1 trillion and would add to the national debt, during the Republican Party's midterm convention over the summer.
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
President Donald Trump during the signing of a security pact between the U.S., Denmark and Greenland during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at U.N. Headquarters Sept. 22, 2026, in New York City. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images / Getty Images)
"Because I delivered on this very important issue for the American People, they can also rest assured the highly popular $5,000 Trump Dividend will be distributed to every U.S. Citizen if, and when, the Republicans win the Midterm Elections!" Trump wrote.
Fox News Digital's Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.
